Since the API is intended for one sidecar, the simplest correct answer is to send no CORS header at all, which leaves browsers unable to read the responses. Then authenticate the routes, so the header stops being the control.

triage.reason: This is the rule the shape usually dies on, and here it does not. The header is not confined to one route: it is set at starter.ts:37 before dispatch, so it applies to all three routes and to the 404 path. There is no narrowing condition anywhere in the handler.
What becomes readable is ledger entries for a named funding account - id, amount, currency and memo (ledger.ts:90) - which is financial record data, not public content.

The intended exposure is stated at starter.ts:82 as the ops console sidecar in the same pod. A wildcard origin is not bounded to that; it admits every origin a browser on the host can load, which is a strictly larger set than the one the comment describes.

scope.established_by: default_resolver.py named the default; the effect list was then established by reading where config.corsOrigin is consumed. grep returns one reader, starter.ts:37, and its position above the route dispatch means the effect list is every response the server emits.
scope.narrowed_by: starter.ts:83 - the listener is bound to 127.0.0.1, so only a browser or process on the host can reach it. That narrows the attacker to code running on the same machine as the service, which for a page in the operator's browser is a normal condition rather than a barrier.

findings.title: The ledger entries endpoint returns any funding account's entries to an unauthenticated caller
findings.evidence: The handler takes accountId straight from the URL path - const [, , accountId, section] = req.url.split('?')[0].split('/') (:64) - and passes it to entriesPage (:69) with no ownership check, no allowlist and no authentication of any kind. The care taken with the neighbouring parameter shows the omission is specific rather than systemic: page is parsed with z.coerce.number().int().min(0).max(50) at :67, while accountId is not validated at all. entriesPage binds it as a parameter (ledger.ts:91), so this is not an injection, but the query filters on nothing except the account the caller named.
findings.impact: Anyone who reaches the port enumerates ledger entries - amount, currency and memo per entry (ledger.ts:90) - for any funding account whose identifier they can supply, 100 rows at a time with an offset they control up to page 50. Account identifiers are UUIDs, but they are also echoed back by the creation endpoint (:46) and appear in memos such as 'rail fee for <entryId>' (payout.ts:113), and a UUID is not an access control.
findings.recommendation: Authenticate the endpoint and scope the query to the accounts the authenticated principal may see, adding the principal to the WHERE clause rather than checking it in the handler. If this API is genuinely for a trusted sidecar only, give the sidecar a credential and verify it; the loopback bind is a deployment detail that F-PAY-05 already shows a browser can cross.

triage.reason: There is no authentication layer at all in this process: the request handler at starter.ts:36-80 is the entire server, and it contains no token check, no session lookup and no middleware. entriesPage applies no scope of its own (ledger.ts:88-95).

The accounts belong to different funding relationships and the endpoint is addressed by account identifier, so a caller reading an account other than the one they are entitled to is a second principal's data. The loopback bind does not remove that: F-PAY-05 establishes a browser path to the port.
The comment at :82 declares the intended exposure as one sidecar, but nothing implements that intent - no credential, no source check, no allowlist. FP-05 requires what bounds it, and nothing does.

scope.established_by: The three routes were enumerated and each read for an authorization check; this is the only read endpoint and it has none. grep for entriesPage returned one caller, starter.ts:69.
scope.narrowed_by: starter.ts:83 - loopback bind, as for F-PAY-05. starter.ts:67 - the page parameter is bounded to 0..50, which caps the rows reachable per account at 5,100 but does not restrict which account.

findings.title: Activity retries defeat idempotency: each rail attempt mints a new idempotency key, and the ledger debit carries none
findings.evidence: The activities are proxied with retry: { maximumAttempts: 3 } (payout.ts:14-17), so Temporal re-invokes the activity function on failure, including on a start-to-close timeout where the first attempt may already have reached the rail. submitPrimary calls newReference() inside the function body (:27) and sends it as the idempotency-key header (:30), so every attempt sends a different key and the rail's deduplication cannot match them. submitCorrespondent has the same structure (:56) and sends no idempotency-key header at all (:59). postEntry has the same exposure on the ledger side: it accepts entry.id, which the workflow populates with the payout id (payout.ts:104), and never uses it - the INSERT at ledger.ts:46-50 lists account_id, amount_minor, currency, memo and kind, and the balance update at :42 is a relative decrement rather than a conditional write. A retry therefore debits the funding account a second time.
findings.impact: A network timeout on a transfer the rail actually accepted causes a second transfer to be submitted under a fresh key, so the beneficiary is paid twice and the funding account is debited twice. The idempotency-key header is present and gives every appearance of protecting against exactly this, which is what makes it worth reporting: the control is there and is defeated by where the value is generated.
findings.recommendation: Derive the reference deterministically from the payout id so every attempt of the same activity sends the same key - pass it in as part of RailRequest, computed once in the workflow, which is deterministic by Temporal's design - and send it on the correspondent rail too. For the ledger, add a unique constraint on an idempotency column populated from entry.id and insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so the second attempt is a no-op rather than a second debit.

triage.reason: The candidate compensating control is the rail's own deduplication, and the code defeats it by construction: dedupe keys on the header value, which differs per attempt. On the ledger side there is no unique constraint visible - the tree contains no migrations or schema - and the code path applies none.
The retry policy at payout.ts:14-17 is unconditional and ships in every build; there is no environment flag on it, and the worker registers the same activities in all environments (worker.ts:10-18).

The scope was checked and is genuinely wide within this service: all three money-moving activities are affected - both rail submissions and the ledger debit - because all three are proxied through the same retry policy at payout.ts:14-17.

scope.established_by: The retry policy at payout.ts:14-17 applies to every activity obtained from that proxyActivities call, which is the full list at :6-13. Each money-moving activity in that list was then read for an idempotency mechanism: submitPrimary sends a key generated per attempt, submitCorrespondent sends none, postEntry ignores the identifier it is given.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. releaseHold (compliance.ts:70-81) and adjustEntry (ledger.ts:65-85) are excluded from applies_to for a different reason - releaseHold's UPDATE is naturally idempotent, while adjustEntry is a relative update that is not, but it runs only on compensation paths where the workflow controls invocation.

findings.title: Dual approval is satisfied by two arbitrary strings in a signal payload, with no check that the approver exists or is entitled
findings.evidence: The approve handler applies exactly one test - that the approver is not the requester - and then stores the approval keyed by the name supplied in the payload: 'if (approval.approver !== input.requestedBy) { approvals.set(approval.approver, approval) }' (:47-51). Approval is an interface of two free strings (:30-33). The release condition counts distinct keys: approvals.size >= 2 (:95). Nothing verifies that an approver is a real person, that they hold an approver role, that they are distinct from each other in any meaningful sense, or that the signal came from an authenticated caller. The requester's own identity is itself unverified upstream - requestedBy is z.string().email() from the request body (starter.ts:19) - so the one check that does exist compares an attacker-supplied name to another attacker-supplied name.
findings.impact: Anyone able to signal the workflow satisfies dual approval by sending two approve signals with any two different strings, for example 'a@x' and 'b@x'. The requester can approve their own payout by using a name different from the one they submitted under. releaseHold then records those strings as the approvers in hold_note (:99, compliance.ts:74), so the audit trail contains the attacker's chosen names and looks correct.
findings.recommendation: Take the approver identity from an authenticated caller rather than from the payload, and check it against a roster of entitled approvers before recording it. Reject an approval whose identity is not in that roster, and record the authenticated principal in the hold note rather than the submitted string.

triage.reason: Signals reach the workflow through the Temporal client, and whether the deployment restricts who may signal this namespace - mTLS, namespace authorization - cannot be established from this tree: worker.ts:6-8 and starter.ts:33 both connect with an address and no credentials, which is consistent with either arrangement. Per the contract this UNKNOWN is what holds the finding at probable rather than confirmed. The in-tree half is not in doubt: lines :47-51 show the workflow recording an approver identity it never validates.

approval.approver is a free string on the signal payload (:30-33) with no schema, no allowlist and no lookup. Its counterpart requestedBy is validated only as an email-shaped string at starter.ts:19, which constrains the format and not the identity.
The control's entire purpose is to require two principals distinct from the requester, so the second principal is definitional here.

scope.established_by: grep for the approve signal and for the approvals map returned the handler at :47, the size test at :95 and the read at :99. Those three sites are the whole of the approval mechanism.
scope.narrowed_by: The approve signal is not exposed by the HTTP server in this tree - starter.ts sends only adjustAmount (:57) - so a caller needs Temporal client access to the payouts namespace rather than merely reaching the loopback port. Whether that access is itself restricted is the UNKNOWN recorded under FP-01.

findings.title: Sidekiq::Web is inserted into the Rack middleware stack at /internal/queues with no authentication, bypassing the authenticated mount declared in routes.rb
findings.class: Broken function-level authorization / exposed admin interface
findings.evidence: The same console is exposed twice with different protection. routes.rb:18-20 mounts it correctly, inside 'authenticate :user, ->(user) { user.platform_admin? }', at /ops/sidekiq. The initializer then adds it a second time as raw middleware - Rails.application.config.middleware.use Sidekiq::Web, "/internal/queues" (sidekiq.rb:34) - which sits in front of the router and so is reached without any route constraint, any Devise session or any role check. The comment above it explains the motivation and confirms the absence: 'The NOC dashboards and the on-call runbooks iframe the queue view from inside the cluster, where they cannot carry a browser session from the main app' (:32-33). Two lines earlier, Sidekiq::Web.set :sessions, false (:30) disables the session that Sidekiq::Web's own CSRF protection depends on. path_coverage.py flagged this independently as DEAD GUARD '/internal/queues' guards nothing: no route starts with it, which is the join between an authorization-shaped path literal and a route table that does not contain it.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the application on that path gets the Sidekiq console: reading job arguments for every queue, which here means partner event payloads, membership rows and manifest arguments, and the console's write actions - retrying, killing and deleting jobs, and triggering scheduled jobs through sidekiq-cron, which routes.rb:4 loads. Retrying a job is arbitrary re-execution of any worker in this application with arguments visible in the interface. With sessions disabled the interface also has no CSRF protection, so a page a logged-in operator visits can drive those actions.
findings.recommendation: Delete the middleware mount at sidekiq.rb:34 and keep the single authenticated mount in routes.rb. If the NOC genuinely cannot carry a browser session, put a credential on that path - a reverse-proxy mTLS client certificate or basic auth via Sidekiq::Web.use Rack::Auth::Basic - rather than removing the check; and re-enable sessions so the console's CSRF protection works.

triage.reason: Nothing in front of it authenticates. Rack middleware added with config.middleware.use runs before the Rails router, so the 'authenticate' constraint at routes.rb:18 cannot apply to it - that constraint is a router-level scope and this mount never reaches the router. Devise's own middleware establishes a warden context but enforces nothing on its own.

The exculpation on offer is the cluster-internal argument in the comment at :32-33, and it is asserted rather than implemented: nothing in the tree binds this path to an internal listener, a separate port or a source-address allowlist. FP-06 requires the boundary named explicitly, and the application serves /internal/queues on the same Puma listener as everything else.

An ingress rule restricting /internal/* could exist outside the repository, but no such artifact was provided. Per FP-08 that is never HOLDS. It does not push this to UNKNOWN either, because the finding does not depend on external reachability: the second, unauthenticated mount is a defect against the first, authenticated one regardless of who can currently reach the path.

scope.established_by: path_coverage.py named the path literal that no route covers. The two mounts were then located by grepping Sidekiq::Web across the tree, which returns the require and mount in routes.rb:3,19, the require and configuration in sidekiq.rb:4,30 and this middleware insertion at :34. Comparing the two mounts is what makes the asymmetry decidable.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing in the repository narrows it. The mount is unconditional - it is not wrapped in an environment check, unlike the development guard the same codebase uses at bulk_invite_worker.rb:19.

findings.title: Partner events pushed onto the queue skip the schema the HTTP path applies, so org.update! becomes mass assignment and role changes escape the allowed set
findings.class: Mass assignment / missing input validation on a second entry path
findings.evidence: The worker documents two entry paths in its own header: events arrive 'either through the signed HTTP endpoint or straight onto the partner_bridge queue from the bridge process' (:3-5), and config/sidekiq.yml:9-11 repeats it - 'The partner bridge writes jobs straight onto this queue with the Sidekiq client protocol'. Only the HTTP path validates. SignedPayload.ingest! verifies the HMAC and then runs EVENT_SCHEMA (signed_payload.rb:46-48), a Dry::Schema that constrains type to three values, role to viewer/dispatcher/supervisor and org_settings to retention_days and timezone only (:17-28), before enqueuing the filtered hash at :50. The queue path enters at perform(payload) (:11) with no schema at all. Inside, two sinks take the payload directly: org.update!(payload["org_settings"]) at :22 passes an arbitrary hash to update!, and InvitePolicy.update_role!(membership, payload["role"]) at :17 passes an arbitrary role string. The comment at :20-21 states the assumption that fails - 'the settings block is already in the shape our Org model expects'.
findings.impact: Anyone able to push a job onto the partner_bridge queue - which per F-DIS-06 needs no signature - updates arbitrary Org columns through update!, since no strong parameters, no permit and no attribute allowlist stands between the payload and the model. That reaches whatever the Org model exposes, and the tree names several security-relevant columns on it: verified_domains (invite_policy.rb:27), seat_limit (:29), bridge_secret (signed_payload.rb:46, :60) and webhook_secret (webhook_dispatch_worker.rb:19). Rewriting bridge_secret or verified_domains dismantles the controls that gate the other paths. Separately, the role restriction that the HTTP schema enforces at :21 is absent, so a queue event sets any role InvitePolicy::ROLES contains, including owner and platform_admin.
findings.recommendation: Validate at the worker rather than at one caller: run EVENT_SCHEMA inside InboundEventWorker#perform so both entry paths pass the same gate, and fail the job when it does not conform. Replace org.update!(hash) with an explicit permitted-attribute list, so a future third entry path cannot reach columns it should not.

triage.reason: The candidate mandatory layer is JobSignatureMiddleware, and it is neither mandatory nor a validator: it is registered only when VERIFY_JOB_ARGS is true, which defaults to false (sidekiq.rb:11, :17), and even when active it checks an HMAC rather than a schema - a correctly signed payload with arbitrary org_settings passes it unchanged (F-DIS-06).

On the queue path the value is the job argument as pushed, with no schema between the queue and :22. The HTTP path does constrain it, which is exactly why the queue path matters: the constraint lives on the path nobody has to take.

The queue is Redis, shared with the client configuration at sidekiq.rb:26-28, and the writer is a process in a partner's VPC per the header comment at :4-5. A partner tenant writing events for its own org is a second principal by definition, and the payload names the org it acts on (:12).

scope.established_by: The two entry paths were enumerated from the worker's own header and from sidekiq.yml:9-11, then each of the three branches of the case statement (:15, :19, :24) was read for what it does with unvalidated payload fields. The shipment.scanned branch was checked too and does not belong here: its carrier value is resolved through a five-entry constant lookup with an early return (:25-26), which is why it appears in ruled_out rather than in this finding.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows the queue path. On the HTTP path the schema at signed_payload.rb:17-28 does narrow both sinks, which is the asymmetry being reported rather than an exculpation.

findings.title: InvitePolicy.update_role! omits the grant ceiling that invite! applies, so a role change can reach roles the granter may not hand out
findings.evidence: The class comment states the design: 'Single place that decides whether an actor may put someone into an org at a given role... both go through +invite!+ so the ceiling and the domain allow-list are applied once' (:3-5). invite! implements it - ROLES membership (:21), the CEILING lookup that restricts what the actor's own role may grant (:23-24), the verified-domain check (:26-27) and the seat limit (:29) - and CEILING is written so that no in-org role can grant platform_admin (:11-16, with the comment at :9-10 saying so explicitly). update_role! sits eleven lines below and applies one of those four checks: 'raise Denied unless ROLES.include?(role)' (:37), then membership.update!(role: role, ...) (:39). It takes no actor parameter at all, so it could not evaluate the ceiling even if it wanted to. Its own comment says it is used by 'the memberships controller and by the partner bridge when an org syncs its directory to us' (:34-35), and the in-tree caller is inbound_event_worker.rb:17.
findings.impact: A role change routed through update_role! can set any of the five roles in ROLES, including owner and platform_admin, with no reference to who is requesting it. Reached through the queue path of F-DIS-02, where the role field is not schema-constrained either, this is a direct path from partner-bridge write access to platform_admin on a membership - the one grant the policy's own comment says nobody may hand out from inside an org.
findings.recommendation: Give update_role! the same signature and the same checks as invite!: take the actor, apply CEILING.fetch(actor.role_in(org), []) before writing, and refuse platform_admin from any in-org path. If a directory sync legitimately needs to bypass the ceiling, give it a named, separate method whose name says so, so the bypass is visible at every call site.

triage.reason: No caller compensates. grep for update_role! returns the declaration and one caller, inbound_event_worker.rb:17, which passes payload["role"] straight through and performs no ceiling check of its own. The memberships controller named in the comment is not present in the tree, so it cannot be credited with the check either.

The scope was checked rather than assumed: the ROLES test at :37 does narrow the input to five known strings, and two of those five - owner and platform_admin - are above what any CEILING entry permits. A filter that admits the values the control exists to exclude is not a narrowing.

The candidate benign reading is that update_role! is only for lateral moves between already-permitted roles. The code says otherwise: it accepts the full ROLES constant (:7, :37) rather than the CEILING values, and the class comment claims the ceiling is applied to both entry points, which is the belief this contradicts.

scope.established_by: The four writers of Membership.role were listed by grep - invite_policy.rb:31, :39, :45 and bulk_invite_worker.rb:35 - and each was read for which of invite!'s four checks it applies. This finding is the :39 writer; the :35 writer is F-DIS-04; the :45 writer is in ruled_out as development-only. writer_parity.py returned 0 flags on this tree, so the asymmetry was established by hand.
scope.narrowed_by: invite_policy.rb:37 - the ROLES membership test bounds the value to five known strings, which prevents arbitrary role names but not privilege escalation.

findings.title: The bulk invite worker writes memberships directly, bypassing the domain allowlist, the seat limit and the grant ceiling that InvitePolicy exists to apply
findings.evidence: The worker builds memberships itself rather than calling the policy: Membership.find_or_initialize_by(org: org, email: email) at :34, then membership.role = role (:35), invited_by (:36), state (:37) and save! (:38). The only check is 'next unless InvitePolicy::ROLES.include?(role)' at :32, which admits all five roles including owner and platform_admin. Three of invite!'s four controls are absent: the CEILING test that limits what the actor may grant (invite_policy.rb:23-24), the verified-domain test on the invitee's email (:26-27) and the seat limit (:29). The role itself comes straight from the uploaded row - role = row["role"].presence || "viewer" (:31) - and the header comment carries the assumption that lets it through: 'The upload is already parsed and validated for shape by the controller' (:3-5). Shape is not authority: a valid CSV row can name any role.
findings.impact: An org owner uploads a CSV and grants platform_admin, the one role InvitePolicy's ceiling explicitly withholds from every in-org role (invite_policy.rb:11-16). The same path invites addresses at domains the org has not verified, which is how an outsider is placed inside an org, and ignores the seat limit that bounds the org's commercial entitlement. The actor check at :17 confirms the caller is an owner and then stops - it establishes who, never what they may grant.
findings.recommendation: Route every row through InvitePolicy.invite!(actor:, org:, email:, role:), rescuing InvitePolicy::Denied per row and reporting the rejected rows in the summary mailer at :44. That restores all four checks in one change and removes the second writer entirely, which is the durable fix: the invariant should not be reachable around.

triage.reason: No layer downstream applies the missing checks. The Membership model is not in the tree, so no model-level validation can be credited - and per FP-08 an unseen validation is UNKNOWN rather than a pass; but the finding does not rest on that, because the policy object that indisputably holds these checks is bypassed at the call site, which is decidable here.
role is row["role"] from the uploaded CSV (:31). The ROLES filter at :32 constrains it to five values, two of which are the escalation.

The unchecked write at :34-38 is the worker's normal production path. The development-only branch in this file is a different construct, the grant_without_checks! call at :19-21 behind Rails.env.development?, and that one is in ruled_out precisely because the flag does exclude it.

scope.established_by: Same join as F-DIS-03: the four writers of Membership.role from grep, each read against the four checks invite! applies. This is the writer at bulk_invite_worker.rb:35, and it is the one that omits the most.
scope.narrowed_by: bulk_invite_worker.rb:17 - 'return unless actor.owner_of?(org)' restricts the path to org owners, so this is an owner exceeding their own ceiling rather than an arbitrary user. The ceiling at invite_policy.rb:12 shows owner is not permitted to grant platform_admin, so the narrowing does not cover the escalation.

findings.title: Server-side request forgery: the webhook worker posts a signed payload to any URL it is handed, with no scheme or destination restriction
findings.evidence: perform takes url as a job argument (:14) and builds a Faraday connection on it directly - Faraday.new(url: url) (:21) - then posts the event body to it (:24-29). There is no scheme allowlist, no host allowlist, no resolution of the host to check it is not private or link-local, no comparison against the org's registered endpoints, and no size or content restriction on the response. The worker's own header states that the destination is not necessarily one of the org's registered endpoints: 'The subscriber may be one of the org's registered endpoints or a one-shot callback the partner asked us to hit' (:5-6), which is the arbitrary-destination case in writing. The response status is written back to a durable record - event.update!(last_status: response.status, ...) at :31-35 - and a non-success status is raised (:37) into Sidekiq's retry, giving eight attempts (:10).
findings.impact: The application makes requests from its own network position to any address a job argument names: cloud metadata at 169.254.169.254, internal admin interfaces, Redis or Postgres on the host, and the unauthenticated Sidekiq console of F-DIS-01 at 127.0.0.1/internal/queues, whose write actions are reachable by POST. The stored last_status turns it into an oracle for probing internal services even when the body is not returned. The request also carries x-dispatch-signature, an HMAC computed with the org's webhook_secret over a body the caller influences (:18-19), so pointing it at an attacker-controlled host yields chosen-plaintext signature pairs for that secret.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the URL and validate before the request: require https, reject any host resolving into private, loopback, link-local or unique-local ranges, and re-check after each redirect. Better, drop the arbitrary-URL feature - look the destination up from the org's registered endpoints by identifier, so the job argument names a row rather than a URL. Route egress through a proxy that enforces the same allowlist so a bypass in application code is not the last line.

triage.reason: url is a job argument with no constraint anywhere on the path to Faraday.new. grep for WebhookDispatchWorker returns only the class definition, so no in-tree caller can be credited with validating it, and the header comment at :5-6 states that one-shot partner-supplied callbacks are an intended input.

No egress control is present in the repository - no proxy configuration, no Faraday middleware beyond the two timeouts at :22-23, no network policy manifest. The signature at :19 authenticates the payload to the receiver and constrains nothing about the destination.

The request originates inside the application's network position and reaches services that are otherwise unreachable to the caller; that difference in trust position is the second principal this class turns on.

scope.established_by: The outbound-HTTP enumeration over the tree returns Faraday in this worker (Gemfile:12, require at :3, use at :21) and the undici calls in payout-orchestrator, which take configured base URLs rather than user input. This is the only outbound client in the tree receiving a caller-supplied URL.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The worker applies its timeouts (:22-23) to every request and no condition guards the destination.

findings.title: Job signature verification is optional twice over: it is disabled by default, and when enabled it skips any payload that simply omits the signature field
findings.class: Control present but inert / authentication bypass
findings.evidence: The middleware verifies only when the payload chooses to be verified: 'if payload.is_a?(Hash) && payload.key?("_sig")' (:58), with the verification inside that branch (:59-60) and an unconditional yield after it (:62). A job whose payload carries no _sig key therefore proceeds unverified - the attacker controls the condition that decides whether the check runs. The middleware is also not registered by default: chain.add(SignedPayload::JobSignatureMiddleware) if VERIFY_JOB_ARGS (sidekiq.rb:17), where VERIFY_JOB_ARGS is ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS", "off") == "on" (:11). The comment states the intent honestly - 'Verification is opt-in per environment while the bridge finishes rolling out signing' (:9-10) - and the default is off. The contrast with the HTTP path is stark: ingest! calls verify! unconditionally and raises SecurityError on mismatch (:46, :36-42).
findings.impact: Every job on the partner_bridge queue is unauthenticated in the default configuration, and remains unauthenticated after the rollout is finished unless the omit-the-field case is also fixed. That is the precondition for F-DIS-02 - anyone with write access to the Redis instance, which sidekiq.rb:7 shows is reached with a password that has a hardcoded fallback, pushes InboundEventWorker jobs and reaches org.update! and update_role!. The second half is the more durable defect, because turning SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS on looks like remediation and changes nothing for an attacker who omits _sig.
findings.recommendation: Make the absence of _sig a failure rather than a skip: raise SecurityError when the key is missing, so verification cannot be opted out of by the caller. Then remove the environment flag and register the middleware unconditionally once the bridge signs; a rollout flag that defaults to off outlives the rollout.

triage.reason: No other layer authenticates queue jobs. Sidekiq's own middleware chain here contains only this and CurrentAttributes::Load (sidekiq.rb:18), and the workers themselves - inbound_event_worker.rb:11, bulk_invite_worker.rb:13 - perform no signature check of their own.

The skip-when-absent branch at :58 ships unconditionally in every environment. The registration flag runs the other way from the FP-04 exculpation: the dangerous configuration is the default, not the excluded one.

This is not an absent defence in depth behind a working control. For jobs that arrive on the queue rather than over HTTP, this middleware is the only authentication that exists, and the HTTP path's verify! does not run for them.

scope.established_by: WEB-27's predicate sweep located the conditional verification; the registration was traced through grep for JobSignatureMiddleware, which returns the class at :55 and the single conditional registration at sidekiq.rb:17, and for VERIFY_JOB_ARGS, which returns the assignment at :11 and that one reader.
scope.narrowed_by: sidekiq.rb:17 - the middleware runs only when SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS is 'on'. That narrows where the second defect (skip-when-absent) is observable, and it is itself the first defect, so the narrowing does not reduce exposure in the default configuration.

findings.title: Arbitrary file write: the manifest filename is joined to the spool path with no containment check and then written by the PDF generator
findings.evidence: filename comes from the job arguments with only a presence test - filename = args["filename"].presence || "#{manifest.reference}.pdf" (:18) - and is joined to the spool directory as target = SPOOL.join(filename) (:26). SPOOL is a Pathname (:13), and Pathname#join has two properties that matter here: a relative argument containing '..' walks up, and an absolute argument replaces the receiver entirely, so join("/etc/cron.d/x") yields /etc/cron.d/x. Neither is checked - there is no realpath, no normalisation, no comparison against SPOOL. The code then actively prepares the escape: FileUtils.mkdir_p(File.dirname(target)) at :27 creates whatever directory the traversal names, and Prawn::Document.generate(target.to_s) at :29 creates and writes the file. The neighbouring parameter shows the difference in care: page is coerced with args["page"].to_i at :17, which is why the interpolated offset at :22 is in ruled_out rather than reported.
findings.impact: Anyone able to enqueue a ManifestRenderWorker job writes a file anywhere the application user can write. The content is partly attacker-influenced - the manifest reference and the stop lines are rendered into the document (:30-33) - but the location alone is enough: writing into config/initializers or any directory Rails eager-loads converts this into code execution on the next boot, and overwriting a cron file, an authorized_keys or a deployment script reaches the same end sooner. Combined with F-DIS-06, enqueuing such a job needs no signature.
findings.recommendation: Do not accept a filename from the caller. Derive it from the manifest - "#{manifest.id}.pdf" - or, if a caller-supplied name is genuinely needed, take the basename only (File.basename(filename)), reject anything that is not a plain name matching a strict pattern, and after joining verify the expanded path is still inside SPOOL before creating any directory or opening any file.

triage.reason: filename is args["filename"] from the job payload (:18). presence rejects nil and empty strings and nothing else; no pattern, no basename, no length bound applies anywhere before :26.

There is no containment layer. Between :18 and the write at :29 the only operations are the join at :26 and the mkdir_p at :27, and the second of those assists the traversal rather than blocking it. Queue-level signing would restrict who can enqueue, but it is off by default (F-DIS-06).

The sink writes to the filesystem: Prawn::Document.generate opens the path for writing and creates it if absent. The fact that the content is a PDF does not bound the damage, because the harm is in the destination - and a PDF's leading bytes do not prevent a Ruby or shell file from being parsed as text with the payload embedded.

scope.established_by: The four Sidekiq perform methods from the boundary enumeration were each read for filesystem and network sinks. This is the only worker that writes a file; grep for FileUtils and for Prawn confirms the write sites are the two lines named.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The filename argument is honoured on every invocation that supplies one, and the fallback at :18 applies only when it is absent.

findings.title: Unescaped partner-controlled event type written into a line-oriented Rails log
findings.evidence: The else branch interpolates the payload's type field straight into a log line: Rails.logger.info("ignoring partner event #{payload['type']}") (:33). Reaching that branch requires a type that matches none of the three known values, which is precisely the attacker-chosen case. On the queue path no schema constrains the field (F-DIS-02), so the value may contain CR and LF; Rails' default logger writes one line per event to a line-oriented file, so an embedded newline forges a record. Note the HTTP path does constrain it - EVENT_SCHEMA restricts type to an included_in? set of three (signed_payload.rb:19) - so a payload reaching :33 with a hostile value has necessarily come through the unvalidated queue path, which makes the two findings one chain. log_escaper.py did not see this line: it reported 0 logging calls across 9 files because it does not parse Ruby, so per WEB-28 the enumeration was kept by hand for this language.
findings.impact: Forged log records: an attacker writes lines that appear to come from the application, which corrupts incident reconstruction and can trigger or suppress alerting rules that match on a prefix. If the aggregator or any log viewer renders these lines as HTML, the same input becomes stored cross-site scripting reached without touching the application. The accountability loss stands even where nothing re-parses the line.
findings.recommendation: Log the value as a structured field rather than interpolating it - Rails.logger.info("ignoring partner event", type: payload['type']) with a JSON formatter - or neutralise control characters at the call site with something like payload['type'].to_s.inspect. Applying the schema at the worker, as F-DIS-02 recommends, also removes the source.

triage.reason: On the queue path the field is unconstrained: perform receives the payload with no schema (:11), and nothing between the queue and :33 filters characters. The HTTP path's included_in? constraint at signed_payload.rb:19 does constrain it, and is recorded in narrowed_by.

The sink is the default Rails logger, which writes newline-delimited text. A structured JSON formatter would change this answer, and none is configured anywhere in the tree - grep returns no formatter, no lograge and no log_formatter assignment.

The rule is answered rather than used to close the finding: even taking the most conservative reading, where no consumer re-parses or renders the line, WEB-28 is explicit that the accountability loss remains. That is what fixes the severity at low here rather than removing the finding.

scope.established_by: Hand enumeration of logging sinks in the two languages log_escaper.py does not parse. grep for Rails.logger across the tree returns two calls: this one and sidekiq.rb:22, which interpolates job['class'] and ex.class - both internal class names rather than caller-controlled strings, so that one is not reported.
scope.narrowed_by: signed_payload.rb:19 - events arriving over the signed HTTP endpoint have type constrained to three literal values, so this is reachable only through the partner_bridge queue path.

findings.title: The Sidekiq Redis URL carries a hardcoded password as its default
findings.evidence: REDIS_URL = ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL", "redis://:sidekiq@localhost:6379/1") (:7). The fallback embeds the password 'sidekiq' in source, and the value is used for both the server and the client connections (:14, :27). ENV.fetch with a default means an unset variable is silently replaced by this value rather than raising, so a misconfigured environment connects with the checked-in credential instead of failing.
findings.impact: A credential in version control is compromised from the moment it is pushed and cannot be rotated by changing the file alone. Where the default is actually used, anyone who knows it reaches the queue - which, given F-DIS-06, means enqueuing unauthenticated jobs and so reaching F-DIS-02 and F-DIS-07. The value being a plausible development password is what makes it likely to survive into an environment where it matters.
findings.recommendation: Use ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL") with no default so a missing variable fails loudly at boot, and rotate the credential, since it has been in the repository's history. Keep any local convenience default in a developer .env file that is not committed.

triage.reason: The line is in a config/initializers file loaded in every environment, not in a test fixture or a development-only block. The file itself demonstrates the alternative: the same codebase gates development behaviour explicitly elsewhere (bulk_invite_worker.rb:19).
The rule concerns attacker-controlled values reaching a sink; this is the opposite direction, a secret value present in source.

The value guards the queue that carries partner event payloads and membership operations, so it is not data without security significance. Its severity is low because the host component is localhost and the credential may well be development-only - not because the class is benign.

scope.established_by: COV-02 key-by-key enumeration of the initializer: each of its five configuration statements was read in turn, which is what surfaced this alongside the unauthenticated mount at :34 in the same file. grep for REDIS_URL returns the assignment and the two consumers.
scope.narrowed_by: sidekiq.rb:7 - the default applies only when SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL is unset; when it is set, the embedded credential is unused, though it remains in the repository's history.

findings.title: Every user may write their own profile document, and the profile is where their role and their org membership are stored
findings.evidence: The rule is 'allow write: if request.auth.uid == uid' (:32), with no constraint on which fields may be written or what values they may take. The document it governs is the one the rest of the rule file derives authority from: profile() reads it (:10-12), role() returns profile().role (:14-16) and memberOf(orgId) returns 'orgId in profile().orgs' (:18-20). Those helpers are the whole authorization model - role() gates writing an org document (:43) and reading the audit trail (:52), and memberOf gates reading an org and everything beneath it (:42, :46). The document's own comment states the contents: 'Display name, home org and role for each inspector' (:28). The application confirms the shape by writing role and orgs on first sign-in (web/src/auth.js:24-31), and since the client SDK writes this document directly, a user can issue the same setDoc with values of their choosing.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user rewrites their own profile with role: 'admin' and orgs containing every org id they wish, and thereby grants themselves what those helpers gate: read and write on any org document (:42-43), read and write on every subcollection of every org through the recursive rule at :45-47 - which is where the field notes actually live - and read access to the audit trail that is otherwise admin-and-auditor only (:52). Self-registration is open (web/src/auth.js:35-39), so this is reachable by anyone who can create an account. It also defeats the server-side membership check in the API, which reads the same self-writable field (functions/index.js:47-50).
findings.recommendation: Stop deriving authority from a user-writable document. Move role and orgs onto custom claims set by a trusted backend and read them from request.auth.token, or keep them in Firestore but write them only with the Admin SDK and make the rule 'allow write: if false'. If the user must edit their own display name, restrict the rule to that field explicitly - request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys().hasOnly(['displayName']) - so role and orgs are immutable from the client.

triage.reason: There is no layer between the client and this document. Firestore security rules are the enforcement layer for direct SDK access, and the web app writes profiles through the client SDK (web/src/auth.js:18, :31). The Cloud Functions do not mediate profile writes - grep shows the functions read profiles (index.js:47) and never write them.

The scope was checked and is not narrower than it reads: the rule covers the whole document, and the two security-bearing fields are read by four separate rules in the same file (:42, :43, :46, :52) plus one server-side check. No condition anywhere restricts which keys the write may touch.
The fields are not display metadata: role decides admin and auditor authority (:43, :52), and orgs decides membership of every org (:19). The comment at :28 lists role among the document's contents.

scope.established_by: The two helper functions that read the profile (role at :14, memberOf at :18) were traced to every rule that calls them, by reading the rule file in full; that call list is the applies_to. The server-side reader was found by grepping profiles/ across the functions.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The write rule carries no field restriction and no value constraint, and every consumer of the two fields trusts them without revalidation.

findings.title: The admin API is deployed with no authentication middleware, while the sibling API in the same file requires a verified ID token
findings.evidence: Two Express applications are built in the same file, twenty lines apart. api registers both middlewares - api.use(corsMiddleware) then api.use(requireIdToken) (:42-43). adminApi registers only the first: adminApi.use(corsMiddleware) at :72, and nothing else. requireIdToken (:17-29) is the function that rejects a missing bearer token and calls admin.auth().verifyIdToken; it is never applied to adminApi, and neither of adminApi's two handlers performs a check of its own (:74-77, :79-82). Both are exported and mounted: exports.adminApi at :111, routed from /admin/** by firebase.json:7. The handlers also carry no membership check, unlike api's own /notes/recent which verifies org membership before reading (:47-50).
findings.impact: GET /admin/orgs/{orgId}/members returns the full member list of any organisation to an unauthenticated caller, and POST /admin/orgs/{orgId}/seats rewrites any organisation's seatLimit. Both run under admin.initializeApp() with the Admin SDK (:7-8), which bypasses the Firestore security rules entirely, so the rule file offers no backstop. cors({ origin: true }) at :15 reflects any requesting origin, so any web page can call these endpoints from a visitor's browser and read the responses; the comment justifying that setting (:10-14) reasons from the token in the Authorization header, which is exactly what this application does not check.
findings.recommendation: Add adminApi.use(requireIdToken) and, above the handlers, an authorization check that the caller is an admin of the org in the path - the tree already has the ingredients at :47-50. Because these run with the Admin SDK, the check has to be explicit; there is no rule file to fall back on. Consider splitting the admin surface into its own deployment with its own ingress restriction rather than mounting it on the public hosting rewrite.

triage.reason: No layer in front authenticates. onRequest at :111 is a plain HTTPS trigger with no auth option, and the hosting rewrite at firebase.json:7 forwards the path without conditions. Firestore rules cannot compensate because the Admin SDK is not subject to them.

The exposure is not bounded: it is published on the same public hosting domain as the marketing app through the /admin/** rewrite, and reflected CORS widens rather than bounds it. Nothing in the tree restricts it to an internal network.
It is exported unconditionally at :111 and wired into firebase.json:7, with no environment flag anywhere on the path. The deploy script at functions/package.json:9 deploys all functions.

scope.established_by: WEB-24's sibling procedure: every route handler in the file was listed from the boundary enumeration, and each was joined to the middleware registered on its own Express app. api's two routes are covered by :43; adminApi's two are covered by nothing. The mount was confirmed against firebase.json's rewrites.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. Both adminApi routes are affected, and neither carries an inline check.

findings.title: The org export callable checks neither authentication nor membership and reads every note in the named org with the Admin SDK
findings.evidence: The callable takes orgId from the request payload and validates only that it is non-empty: 'const orgId = String(request.data?.orgId || \'\'); if (!orgId) throw new HttpsError(...)' (:89-92). request.auth is never consulted - a Firebase onCall handler receives it when the caller is signed in and undefined otherwise, and neither branch is checked here - and no membership comparison is made against the caller's profile. The query then reads up to 5000 documents from orgs/{orgId}/notes (:94) through the Admin SDK (:7-8), which is not subject to the security rules. The contrast is one file away: the sibling REST handler for the same data loads the caller's profile and returns 403 when orgId is not in profile.orgs (:47-50). The docstring acknowledges the elevated privilege and gives the reason - 'Runs with the Admin SDK because the export spans every inspector's notes in the org' (:84-87) - which explains why it is privileged and not why it is unguarded.
findings.impact: Anyone who can invoke the callable exports every field note of any organisation whose id they can name: id, ownerId, status, title and body for up to 5000 notes per call (:97). Field notes are inspection records with site references and free-text bodies, so this is the service's entire content across tenant boundaries. Org ids are not secret - they are handled client-side throughout (web/src/notes.js:18-19, web/src/share.js:19) and appear in the download filename (share.js:49).
findings.recommendation: Reject an unauthenticated call - if (!request.auth) throw new HttpsError('unauthenticated', ...) - and then verify membership the way the REST sibling does, by loading profiles/{request.auth.uid} and requiring orgId in its orgs, plus whatever role the export ought to demand. Since the profile is client-writable today, fix F-FIE-01 as well or the membership check rests on a value the caller controls.

triage.reason: Callable functions apply no authorization of their own; they surface request.auth for the handler to check, and this handler does not. The Firestore rules that would otherwise gate orgs/{orgId}/notes (firestore.rules:45-47) do not apply, because the read goes through the Admin SDK.

Nothing bounds the exposure. The callable is exported at :88 and reachable by any client of the Firebase project; the web app invokes it through httpsCallable (web/src/share.js:5), which shows the ordinary caller is the browser.
The exported fields include each note's ownerId, title and body (:97) - identified inspection content, which the rest of the design treats as owner-restricted (firestore.rules:34-38).

scope.established_by: The three privileged entry points in the functions file were enumerated (api, adminApi, exportOrgNotes) and each was read for an authentication check and a membership check. exportOrgNotes has neither; api has both at :43 and :47-50; adminApi has neither and is F-FIE-02.
scope.narrowed_by: functions/index.js:94 - the query is capped at 5000 documents per call and scoped to one org per call, so extraction is per-org and paginated by repetition rather than unbounded in a single request.

findings.title: The seal endpoint writes the immutable audit trail at a caller-chosen document id, with no membership check and no merge
findings.class: Audit trail tampering / broken object-level authorization
findings.evidence: The audit id is built entirely from caller-supplied values: 'const { orgId, seq } = normalizeRequest(req.body); const auditId = `${orgId}_${seq}`' (:60-61), where normalizeRequest coerces but does not restrict them (:32-39). The write is db.doc(`audits/${auditId}`).set({...}) at :62-67 - .set without { merge: true }, so it replaces any existing document at that id. No check confirms the caller belongs to orgId, and none confirms the note in the path belongs to that org or to the caller. The sibling handler in the same Express app does exactly that check for a read: /notes/recent loads the profile and returns 403 unless orgId is in profile.orgs (:47-50). The collection is declared immutable in the rules - 'Immutable trail written by the audit function with the Admin SDK' with allow write: if false (firestore.rules:50-54) - and that guarantee holds only for direct client access, because this function writes through the Admin SDK.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user overwrites any audit record by naming its org and sequence number, destroying the record of who sealed what and replacing it with their own uid and a note id of their choosing. They can also seal notes in organisations they do not belong to. The audit trail is the evidentiary artifact in an inspection system - the one collection the rules single out as immutable - and the only writer to it accepts its primary key from the request body.
findings.recommendation: Derive the audit id server-side: use an auto-generated id, or a deterministic one built from the note id and a server timestamp, so the caller cannot choose where the write lands. Use .create() rather than .set() so an existing record cannot be replaced, and add the membership check the sibling handler already performs, verifying both that the caller is in orgId and that noteId belongs to it.

triage.reason: The rules' allow write: if false (firestore.rules:53) is the candidate control and it does not reach this path: the Admin SDK bypasses security rules by design, which is stated in the collection's own comment at :50. No other check exists between :60 and the write at :62.

Both components of the key are attacker-controlled. normalizeRequest strips orgId to [A-Za-z0-9_-] (:34), which prevents path traversal into another collection but leaves the caller free to name any org, and seq is Number(body.seq) || 0 (:35) with no bound at all.

The scope was checked: this handler is behind requireIdToken (:43), so the caller must be signed in. That narrows the attacker set to any registered user - and registration is open (web/src/auth.js:35-39) - while leaving every audit document in every org writable.

scope.established_by: grep for audits across the tree returns two sites: this write and the read rule at firestore.rules:51-54. That makes this the sole writer, and the rule file's allow write: if false confirms no other client path exists.
scope.narrowed_by: functions/index.js:43 - requireIdToken applies to this Express app, so a valid Firebase ID token is required. No membership or ownership condition narrows it further.

findings.title: A recursive wildcard grants every org member read and write on every document beneath the org, overriding the per-note ownership model
findings.evidence: Inside the orgs match, a recursive wildcard grants 'allow read, write: if memberOf(orgId)' (:45-47), covering every subcollection and every document at any depth. The notes actually live there: the client writes to collection(db, 'orgs', orgId, 'notes') (web/src/notes.js:18-19), the storage rules look a note up at orgs/$(orgId)/notes/$(noteId) (storage.rules:9) and the functions query orgs/{orgId}/notes (functions/index.js:52, :94). Meanwhile the rules that express the intended ownership model - 'A field note belongs to the inspector who took it', allow read/update/delete only if resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid (:34-39) - are written against the top-level collection /notes/{noteId}, which nothing in the tree reads or writes. The ownership model is therefore declared on a path that holds no data, and the path that holds the data is governed by plain membership.
findings.impact: Any member of an org reads, edits and deletes every other inspector's field notes in that org, contrary to the model the rule file states one section earlier. The wildcard also covers the members subcollection that the admin API reads (functions/index.js:75) and any other administrative subcollection, so a plain member can write documents the org document itself reserves for admins - :43 requires role() == 'admin' to write orgs/{orgId}, and :46 then grants write on everything under it to any member. Combined with F-FIE-01, where a user can add any org id to their own profile, membership is self-granted and this rule turns that into read/write across that org's entire data.
findings.recommendation: Delete the recursive wildcard and write explicit rules per subcollection. Move the ownership rules onto the path the data actually uses - match /orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId} with the memberOf check for create and the ownerId comparison for read, update and delete - and give members and other administrative subcollections their own rules requiring role() == 'admin'. Then remove the dead /notes/{noteId} block so the file stops describing a model it does not enforce.

triage.reason: For direct client SDK access, which is how this app reads and writes notes (web/src/notes.js:22-53), the rules are the only enforcement layer. There is no server intermediary on that path to reimpose ownership.

This is the rule to ask hardest here and the answer is no. A narrowing condition would be the /notes/{noteId} block at :35-39, and it does not narrow this path: it matches a different, unused collection. The recursive wildcard has no condition beyond memberOf.

The candidate benign reading is that /notes/{noteId} is the collection in use and the wildcard covers something else. Four independent sites contradict it - notes.js:18-19, storage.rules:9, index.js:52 and index.js:94 - all addressing orgs/{orgId}/notes.

scope.established_by: Every collection path used anywhere in the tree was collected from the client code, the functions and the storage rules, then matched against the rule file's match blocks. That join is what shows /notes/{noteId} matching nothing and orgs/{orgId}/{document=**} matching the notes, the members subcollection and everything else beneath an org.
scope.narrowed_by: firestore.rules:19 - the grant requires memberOf(orgId), so it is org members rather than all users. F-FIE-01 shows membership is self-assignable, which is why that narrowing is thin, but it is real and is recorded here rather than omitted.

findings.title: Storage allows any authenticated user to overwrite any note attachment, with none of the checks that create requires
findings.evidence: Within one match block, four operations are declared and one is the odd one out. read requires the caller to be the note's owner (:12); create requires ownership plus a 15 MB size limit plus a content type matching image/.* or application/pdf (:14-17); delete requires ownership (:22). update requires only 'request.auth != null' (:20) - no ownership, no size limit, no content type. The comment above it explains the intent, 'Re-uploading a photo after the inspector rotates or crops it in the app' (:19), which describes the owner re-uploading their own file and is not what the rule expresses. Because the object path is orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}/{fileName} (:6), overwriting requires only knowing or guessing that path, and note ids are handed to clients throughout the app (web/src/notes.js:41, :60).
findings.impact: Any authenticated user replaces the evidentiary photograph or PDF attached to any inspection note in any organisation, including orgs they do not belong to, since update does not even call noteOwner(). The replacement is unconstrained in size and type, so the same rule permits uploading arbitrary content - executable or HTML - under a path whose download URL is treated as trusted by the app, and permits storage exhaustion with no cap. In an inspection system the integrity of the attachment is the point of the record.
findings.recommendation: Give update the same conditions as create: noteOwner() == request.auth.uid, the size limit and the contentType match. The three conditions already exist eight lines above, so this is a copy rather than a design decision. Consider disallowing update entirely and having the app write a new object, which keeps the original evidence intact.

triage.reason: Storage rules are the enforcement layer for direct SDK uploads, and the app uploads directly - uploadBytes(target, file, ...) at web/src/notes.js:61. No function mediates the write; grep shows no storage access in functions/index.js at all.

The scope is narrow in path terms - one match block - and not narrowed in principal terms, which is what matters here: within that block, update applies to every object of every note of every org, for every authenticated user. The sibling operations in the same block are the evidence that a narrowing was intended and omitted.
The objects are note attachments - inspection photographs and PDFs - governed elsewhere in the same file by an owner check (:12, :22), which is the file's own statement that they are not public.

scope.established_by: The four allow declarations inside the single match block at :6 were listed and their conditions compared side by side. The other match block in the file, /exports/{orgId}/{fileName}, denies everything (:25-27) and needs no comparison.
scope.narrowed_by: storage.rules:20 - the caller must be authenticated. Registration is open (web/src/auth.js:35-39), so that is any account holder.

findings.title: The shared-note view assigns the note body to innerHTML while every other field on the same page uses textContent
findings.evidence: The function renders four values from the note and treats one differently. The heading uses heading.textContent = note.title (:30), and the site reference and status go through field(), which also uses textContent (:9, :11). The body is assigned as markup: article.innerHTML = note.body (:39). note.body is stored unsanitised - createNote writes the body straight from its argument (web/src/notes.js:31-36) and updateNote spreads the patch into the document (:44-48); grep across the tree finds no sanitiser, no DOMPurify and no escaping on any path into that field. The comment above the function describes both the audience and the provenance without connecting them: the view is 'a read-only view of a note for the share link a supervisor sends to the site contact', and 'The body is authored in the app's rich-text field' (:15-18).
findings.impact: Script stored in a note body executes in the browser of whoever opens the share link, in the application's origin. That is enough to act as the viewer against Firestore with their credentials - reading and writing whatever their profile permits - and, because profiles are self-writable and read for authority (F-FIE-01), to escalate from there. The audience makes it worse: the link is deliberately sent to external site contacts, and F-FIE-05 means any org member, not only the note's author, can plant the payload in someone else's note.
findings.recommendation: Render the body as text with textContent, as the three fields around it already do. If rich text is a real requirement, sanitise with an allowlist library immediately before the assignment and store the source separately from the rendered output, so the sanitiser runs on every read rather than once on a write path that another writer can skip.

triage.reason: note.body traces to the client-supplied argument of createNote (notes.js:29-36) and to any key in the patch object of updateNote (notes.js:44-48). Neither applies a filter, and the Firestore rules constrain who may write the document, not what the field may contain.
innerHTML parses its argument as HTML by definition, which is precisely the distinction the same function draws by using textContent for the other three fields.

No sanitiser sits anywhere on the path. grep for sanitize, DOMPurify, escape and bleach across the fieldnotes tree returns nothing, and no Content-Security-Policy is configured - firebase.json's headers block sets only Cache-Control on static assets (:10-15).

scope.established_by: The DOM-sink enumeration over the tree returned exactly one innerHTML assignment. The writers of note.body were then listed by grep across web/src, giving createNote and updateNote, and both were read for sanitisation.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The assignment is unconditional and runs for every note the shared view renders.

findings.title: The admin API interpolates the raw path parameter into Firestore document paths, where an encoded slash can redirect the write
findings.evidence: The two adminApi handlers build Firestore paths from req.params.orgId with no sanitisation: db.collection(`orgs/${req.params.orgId}/members`) at :75 and db.doc(`orgs/${req.params.orgId}`) at :80. The sibling application sanitises the same value before using it - normalizeRequest strips everything outside [A-Za-z0-9_-] at :34, and api's handlers use the result (:46, :60) - so the omission is specific to adminApi rather than a house style. Express decodes percent-escapes into req.params, so a request to /admin/orgs/acme%2Fnotes%2Fn1/seats yields orgId = 'acme/notes/n1' and the template at :80 becomes db.doc('orgs/acme/notes/n1'), a four-segment and therefore valid document path. The write that follows is a merge set of seatLimit (:80) performed with the Admin SDK, so the security rules do not intervene.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller - the endpoint has no authentication at all, F-FIE-02 - writes a seatLimit field into a document of their choosing rather than the intended org document, for example onto a note or another org's record, corrupting arbitrary data through a rules-bypassing SDK. The read handler at :75 has the same shape and can be pointed at other collections whose path arithmetic works out to an odd number of segments.
findings.recommendation: Apply the sanitiser the file already has: run req.params.orgId through the same [A-Za-z0-9_-] filter as normalizeRequest, or better, validate it against a known-org lookup before using it in a path. Compose paths segment by segment - db.collection('orgs').doc(orgId) - so a separator in the value cannot change the shape of the reference.

triage.reason: The value is a URL path parameter used verbatim; no filter, pattern or lookup is applied on either adminApi handler. The sanitised sibling at :34 proves the value is regarded as untrusted elsewhere in the same file.

Whether Express decodes %2F into req.params before the route matches, and whether the firebase-admin path parser accepts the resulting embedded separators rather than rejecting them, could not be verified from this tree - neither library's source nor a runtime was available, and outside information is out of scope for this run. Per the contract this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is why it is not reported as confirmed. What is certain in-tree is the unsanitised interpolation and the sibling that sanitises.
The Admin SDK bypasses the Firestore rules (:7-8), so the rule file cannot bound where the write lands, and no other check exists in either handler.

scope.established_by: Every Firestore path template in the functions file was listed and each was classified by whether its interpolated value had passed normalizeRequest. Four templates use the sanitised value (:47, :52, :62, :94); two use the raw parameter, and both are on adminApi.

findings.title: The CSV export concatenates note fields without quoting or escaping, producing both formula injection and field corruption
findings.evidence: Each row is built as [doc.id, note.ownerId, note.status, note.title, note.body].join(',') (:97) and prefixed with a header line (:100). No value is quoted, no embedded comma or quote is escaped, no newline is stripped, and no leading =, +, - or @ is neutralised. title and body are free text written by users through createNote and updateNote (web/src/notes.js:31-48). The result is handed to the browser and saved as a .csv file (web/src/share.js:45-50), which is a filename and MIME type that spreadsheet applications open directly.
findings.impact: A note title beginning with = is interpreted as a formula when the export is opened in a spreadsheet, which is the standard vector for data exfiltration through functions like WEBSERVICE and HYPERLINK and, with the user's confirmation, for command execution through DDE. Separately and with no attacker required, any comma or newline in a legitimate note body shifts every following column, so the export silently misreports which inspector owns which note - a correctness problem in a file that is presumably used for reporting.
findings.recommendation: Use a CSV serialiser rather than join: quote every field, double any embedded quote, and prefix any value beginning with =, +, - or @ with a single quote or a tab so spreadsheets treat it as text. The same change fixes both the injection and the column shifting.

triage.reason: title and body come from user input with no constraint anywhere: createNote passes them through unmodified (notes.js:31-36) and no schema or length limit exists on either field in the rules or the client.

The sink is a file the application labels text/csv and names <org>-notes.csv (share.js:45, :49), so the intended consumer is a spreadsheet application, which is the interpreter this class turns on. The column-shifting half of the impact does not depend on any interpreter at all.
The export carries ownerId, title and body for every note in an org, and F-FIE-03 establishes it can be pulled for any org, so the file is neither public nor synthetic.

scope.established_by: The single CSV-producing site in the tree was located by reading exportOrgNotes end to end after it had already yielded the authorization finding (F-FIE-03) - the COV-01 return to a file that had already produced something. grep confirms no other join(',') or csv construction anywhere.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. Every row of every export goes through this line.

findings.title: Every signed-in user can read every inspector's profile document
findings.evidence: The rule is 'allow read: if signedIn()' (:30), where signedIn() is only 'request.auth != null' (:6-8), with no membership or ownership condition. The documents contain displayName, email, role and orgs, which ensureProfile writes on first sign-in (web/src/auth.js:24-31) and the rule file's own comment describes as 'Display name, home org and role for each inspector' (:28).
findings.impact: Any account holder enumerates the email address, role and org memberships of every user of the platform across all organisations. That is a personal-data disclosure in itself and it is also reconnaissance for the escalation paths in this service: knowing which uid holds role 'admin' and which orgs exist tells an attacker exactly which values to write into their own profile under F-FIE-01, and which org ids to name in F-FIE-03.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the read to the document's owner and to whatever narrower audience the app genuinely needs - for example, allow read if request.auth.uid == uid || memberOf of a shared org - and move email out of the client-readable document if only the backend needs it.

triage.reason: The documents contain email addresses tied to named individuals, which is personal data, together with role and org membership. This is not public reference data - the file's own catalog collection at :22-26 is what that looks like here.
Nothing bounds the exposure to an intended audience: signedIn() admits every authenticated user of the project, and registration is open (web/src/auth.js:35-39).

The rule is answered rather than used to close the finding. The impact does reach users - their email and role are readable by strangers - which is why it is reported; its severity is low because it is disclosure rather than modification, and because the modification half of the same rule block is reported separately and at high severity as F-FIE-01.
